March 11, 1974
The House resumed at 2 p.m.

['Mr. Speaker, it is my understanding that the House leaders will be meeting again on Wednesday.\nAt 9.46 p.m. the House adjourned, without question put, pursuant to Standing Order.', 'Tuesday, March 12, 1974']

Mr. Speaker, before we recessed for lunch I was referring to Canada Manpower centres and I was levelling something of a barrage against the inefficiency of their operations across this country. I will continue now with my address.
Another negative aspect about the manpower centres' poor performance over the years is that it has been bad for morale among CMC employees who often feel a sense of helplessness and frustration. Indeed, as a result of a recent questionnaire sent out to manpower employees, it was found that a substantial percentage felt that, despite changes and so-called reforms within manpower operations, their work had not improved, nor had their services improved. Hardly a day goes by that I do not get a letter or telephone call from an unemployed constituent complaining that manpower "is doing nothing for me". This may be due to ignorance on the part of some job seekers or it may be an exaggeration, but the important thing is that the impression is left that manpower is somehow failing them. This feeling did not occur overnight; it has built up over the years. So, obviously, there is some truth to the allegation.
I also receive criticism from some employers who are hard pressed for employees, although some of these complaints come from employers who cannot or will not pay more than minimum wages. I will have something more to say on this point later, when I will make a positive suggestion for a solution to this one aspect of manpower's many problems.
One of the most demoralizing situations within many Canada Manpower centres is the heavy workload that counsellors must endure, particularly in the large metropolitan centres. As late as 1973, I am told on good authority, some counsellors were responsible for as many as 400 or 500 cases at a time. No wonder that in 1972 CMC placed only 11 per cent of those who sought employment. It is my understanding that this problem is being resolved, but many CMC personnel must still waste valuable time cutting their way through endless red tape instead of being able to devote more time to a person to person counselling relationship with employees and employers.
The constituency I have the honour to represent contains many tobacco and vegetable farmers. In recent years these rural employers have been finding it increasingly difficult to obtain sufficient numbers of workers and each spring I am deluged with complaints alleging inefficiency and indifference on the past of Canada Manpower centres. I know that it is difficult these days to attract people, particularly young people, to work on farms. Many farmers cannot compete with urban industries with respect to wages; working conditions on some farms leave much to be desired; and many young people just do not want to slug it out in the fields.
I am not, therefore, entirely blaming Canada Manpower centres for this shortage of labour, but farmers, who have enough worries to begin with, must be assured, before planting and harvesting, that they will have sufficient help. This means that if unemployment is down to about 3.5 per cent in southwestern Ontario, as it has been in
The Address-Mr. Blackburn
recent months, leaving mainly older people and those with very poor work records searching for work, there must be greater mobility during crisis periods, not just of bodies but of reliable help. If we must import farm workers, we must increase the quotas and at the same time ensure that these imported workers are not exploited by a few unscrupulous farmers who give all farmers a bad name.
I should like now to return to the whole question of institutional versus on-the-job training to which I alluded earlier when I argued against present methods and strategies. It is my opinion that there must be greater co-operation between industry and business on the one hand, and our school systems on the other. Industry must take a more responsible role in the training of its employees and schools must give up some of their control over the education of those students who are in the industrial and business streams in the various school systems. I see a very real need for establishing a new apprenticeship system involving the federal government through manpower and the provincial governments and local school boards. Admittedly, there is a constitutional problem here, but I am sure legal and jurisdictional obstacles could be overcome.
My argument is based on the premise that more students at the secondary school level should be screened into industrial, business and other vocational programs and fewer into the purely academic. I should state at this point that while some parents might object to this early streaming, I think in the long run our young people would be much happier, the cost of educating a large proportion of our young would be considerably less, and our students would be much better prepared to enter the work force. I should also emphasize at this point that I am not suggesting that such an apprenticeship program be a mechanism to reduce employment, as were the LIP and OFY Programs. It should not be a "make work" program. Quite the contrary, it should be a well structured and positive program to challenge our young people to learn important skills and trades for a labour market that needs them. Mechanics, machinists, tool and dye makers, various kinds of office skills, and commercial and business positions are in great demand.
What I propose is that after the age of about 15, those best suited for industrial work or secretarial and business occupations, spend half the school day or half the school week in a work-training situation, learning skills that are directly related to changing conditions in industry and business, not to jobs that may be obsolete or redundant in ten years' time. The trainees, of course, would not be thrown to the mercy of a tough boss whose only aim was to get as much sweat out of them at the lowest possible subsidized wages. Rather, all trainees would be under the umbrella of local boards of education and local manpower centres. Supervisors from both the local CMC and board of education would oversee the program. Employers would be subsidized to some extent but the emphasis would be placed on wages for services performed while the student was learning a skill. Apart from learning a useful skill or trade and earning an income at the same time he is attending school, the student would gain a greater sense of responsibility and achievement.

March 11, 1974
The Address-Mr. Blackburn
It is indeed, Mr. Speaker, a sad commentary on modern educational techniques in Canada today that so many of our young people have become so disillusioned, not only about work, but about life in general. I do not blame the schools alone, but certainly they must share in the blame. Far too many of our young people approach life with indifference and apathy, wandering in a society that on the one hand damns them for being cynical and lazy, but on the other, gives them so little incentive to be productive citizens. This holds true, of course, for older people in the work force, who have become the victims of job obsolescence without any meaningful alternatives except, to a considerable degree, equally obsolescent manpower retraining schemes, or even worse, a life ahead of jumping from one job to another and living on social assistance between jobs.
Another area where Canada Manpower could improve its operations is in the north. It is painfully obvious that there is a lack of firm policy with respect to settling the north as well as developing it with well-trained personnel who will remain in the more remote areas of Canada as well adjusted people.
There are horrendous implications as both highly skilled professionals as well as tradesmen and labourers prefer the amenities and advantages of working and living in southern cities because of their relative comfort and social and cultural diversities. Obviously, the native peoples of the north should be given preference for jobs if they want to accept the white man's socio-economic work ethic. But greater encouragement should also be given to people from southern communities as well. If Siberia can be developed, then Canada's north can be, too. I am not here referring to slave labour camps, either.
It seems to me, Mr. Speaker, that in order to encourage Canadians to move north, provided there is suitable employment-and here we should be very careful to see there is guaranteed employment-certain steps should be taken. Not only should salaries and wages be higher, but these added benefits should not be wiped out by higher living costs so that in reality the northern worker is no better off materially than he would be if he remained in southern Canada. This, of course, is the major problem today. People move north because they are attracted by higher wage offers, and when they get there they find out that a loaf of bread or a quart of milk is five cents, ten cents or twelve cents higher than it is at home. Moreover, cheaper housing should be made available. No longer should there be paid holidays spaced throughout the year, including travelling expenses to southern Canada. I would also suggest higher income tax exemptions for those working in the remote areas of northern Canada.
I now come to one aspect relating to Canada Manpower that I find serious and unacceptable, in fact it is an insult to Canada Manpower itself. I am referring to the practice of government departments hiring what is termed "casuals" through private placement agencies, not through their own hiring agency, Canada Manpower. On any given day it is estimated there are 1,500 persons working as casuals in various government offices. The private placement agencies charge anything from 33'A per cent to 50 per cent, based either on the first day's salary or on a continuing basis, as long as the casual job exists. Mr. Speaker, some of 
these so-called casuals work for months. It is reported that one actually worked for two years and was still classified as casual. The average duration of the job is about two weeks. It is estimated that the total bill the government pays to these private placement agencies is about $8 million to $9 million a year, of which approximately $3 million goes in fees to the private agencies.
I have nothing against private placement agencies, Mr. Speaker, but why should the government not use its own Manpower facilities? And this could be done. I am not in the habit of praising the Ontario government because I do not often find anything to praise, but I would like to make the point that it has set up its own bureau or pool for casuals and charges the Ontario treasury only 5 per cent, not 33'A per cent or 50 per cent as the federal government is paying for casual workers. I suggest this kind of setup also has UIC implications as well. It encourages casuals to work only one day a week, say for $25 and still collect unemployment insurance, though I am told that the placement agencies try to prevent this.
Mr. Speaker, I was going to continue by discussing unemployment insurance in more detail but I realize that my time is running short so I shall not present that section of my speech.

Mr. Speaker, I am very happy to join those who have participated in this debate in congratulating His Excellency the Governor General and his wife on their appointment. The qualities they bring are the guarantee that they will perform their duties with dignity. I also join my colleagues in congratulating the movers of the Address in Reply to the Speech from the Throne, the hon. member for Spadina (Mr. Stollery) and the hon. member for Sherbrooke (Mr. Pelletier): they had a rather difficult task and they performed it well.
During this debate, I had the opportunity of hearing several of the speeches made by hon. members of the government and of the opposition, party leaders, ministers and ministerial hopefuls. However, I noticed that few solutions had been found to at least a reasonable percentage of the many problems now confronting the Canadian people.
I noted carefully the contents of the Speech from the Throne at the opening of this session and noticed that while it summarized good intentions, it gave few specifics on the means the government intends to use to improve the situation.
Our administrators are suffering from the inflationary fever they helped give rise to and maintain without trying to improve the situation. Our financial system is sick; it has grown into a cancer that feeds ceaselessly on the economic blood of the nation.
Our specialists, or those who think they are, try to give us the impression that they hope to find cures to the ills of society.
Evidence is such that they cannot deny the existence of economic unease. Still, the results of their research prove that there are too many doctors attending the patient.

Many of them have already admitted their inability to find solutions; they would have the people believe that the illness is international. That is easy to say, but by no means a solution.
Others, who aspire to the leadership of this country, advocate a price freeze, without foreseeing what would happen when the thaw comes. They should at least define their intentions.
I shall attempt to outline some aspects of the present economic situation which further complicate life for Canadians and whose ill effects, that are often demoralizing, could be alleviated through a better balanced distribution system.
Politicians are unable, it seems, to explain the fact that there are poor people who live miserably in a rich country. We see that the previous generation did not waste its time and that today's asserts itself through its knowledge in various fields.
There is however a fly in the ointment. Having reached peaks in the area of production and communication, we are unable to set up exchange methods for available goods.
Instead of basing our economic system on logic, according to a natural order, we remain stuck with a system of scarcity of means to distribute the existing wealth, with the result that thousands of Canadians live in slums even though we have enough materials available to build decent housing.
Many Canadians must depend on welfare not to starve in a country that can advertise through every possible means a whole variety of products.
I do not think it is necessary to have attended university to admit that man has been created with needs to be filled; the need to eat, to dress, to have a home, to love, to help each other and to unite. These needs were not instilled into man by politicians or financiers. All proceeded from creation. The natural right to live existed well before the formation of political parties or unions. We also admit that the Creator in His wisdom has provided for all our needs and we are fortunate in Canada to have abundant resources. The Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce (Mr. Gillespie) travels in various countries to offer our excess production.
Our problems are not due to our inability to produce or build, but rather to our ability to pay. We have the physical capacity, but we do not have the financial means. Our production system is satisfactory, but our financial system is inadequate. This question is always with us and should be looked into more fully than it has been up to now in order to develop a mechanism which would make financially possible what is morally good and physically possible. If we really want to build a better future than today we will have to further our investigations in that respect.
This government has submitted a list of various bills it intends to introduce in this House in the second session of this 29th Parliament. I hope those bills will be drafted in a comprehensible style, thus avoiding the many difficulties that generally flow from bills that are too complicated which inevitably result in problems of comprehension and interpretation that often require for those who would want to take advantage of them the services of legal
The Address-Mr. Dionne
advisers to define what are the rights and privileges of each and everyone.
The 1971 Unemployment Insurance Act will undoubtedly have to be amended. I read recently in Da Presse an article where the chairman of that group was reported as having put the UIC back on the track. One can only infer that it had been off the track for a while. The whole thing was operating strangely. I would hope that the methods of application and the amendments brought in will not be too complicated by technocrats who never experienced the difficulties faced by the unemployed. A situation of confusion was created with the results we know-months of backlog in the payment of benefits, overpayments, double payments, or no payment at all, for all sorts of reasons one as trivial as the other. Eligibility was compromised because of supplement periods, reference periods, extension periods, severance periods, holiday credits considered as gains. To complete the picture payments were centralized through a team of push-button civil servants who were fed often distorted statistics and who tried to control more or less-often less than more-by operating computers overloaded with income tax calculations which resulted in increasing errors and hardships for the unemployed.
I also noted at items 14 and 15 of the list of legislative measures two bills dealing with banks-one to amend the Bank Act and the other to set up a Federal Business Development Bank.
My colleague, the hon. member for Villeneuve (Mr. Tetrault), explained in the House on March 7 the role of the present banking system with figures supporting his thesis. Let us hope that legislators will take into account the fact that man was created before money, that the latter is only an instrument of exchange and its role is to serve and not to enslave. We must establish a real mechanism for the distribution of wealth.
In the Speech from the Throne, there is also a measure concerning the status of women. Let us hope that we will recognize the necessity of establishing a satisfactory balance as regards women's rights so that they can benefit from the advantages they deserve.
There is also a measure creating a federal commission on human rights. I would like to note that there is already a Canadian Bill of Rights. However, the right to economic advantages are not mentioned in this bill. Freedom in its various forms is discussed, but political rights are involved and we know that the latter are often used to the detriment of others' right. There seems to be a tendency to claim rights while ignoring important duties. I regret to note this serious gap in previous bills of human rights. They don't deal with the economic rights of the individual. It is nevertheless logical to conclude that, if any individual has a right to live, he must have therefore a right to the goods which are necessary to life.
We are favoured with a wealth of all kinds of goods but apparently we are not clever enough to find a way of distributing the goods which are available to us and which could be multiplied by modern means of production which improve continuously.

March 11, 1974
The Address-Mr. Dionne
The Speech from the Throne also deals with amendments to be brought to the Canada Pension Plan. I read from the speech and I quote:
The federal and provincial governments have agreed that the Canada and Quebec Pension Plans should be further amended to provide for increases, beyond 1975, in the levels of income upon which contributions may be made, and in the pensions which will be paid. Legislation will be introduced to remove the earnings test now required for people aged 65 to 69 from the Canada Pension Plan. Finally, federal and provincial ministers have agreed that the provisions which now accord differential treatment to men and women under the Canada and Quebec Pension Plans should be removed.
Several improvements will have to be brought. When revising the pension plan, it would be quite normal to try to examine the possibilities, and I know there are some, of establishing the retirement age at 60.
Several countries have already brought down the retirement age to 60: Denmark, New Zealand, Australia. And so it is in other countries too. Very often we follow the example of various countries. Let us follow it for good things, and not only for bad things.
Young people who don't work now and get discouraged would find, thanks to vacant positions, the work that would help them spend their energies, use up their time and give them hope to settle down and raise a family. Finally, the young people would find their ideals instead of losing them, as it happens at present.
Is it not a shame, in a nation like ours, that a family head of 60 years be compelled to provide a living to unemployed of 20 or 25 years. The contrary would be more in keeping with standards. In a country as rich and as prosperous as ours, it is normal that people retire at 55 or 60, but to find idle men aged 20, 25, or 30 is abominable and discreditable.
I would not conclude my remarks without saying a word about energy which has been talked about so much. I know there is a lot more to say on this matter. I had the opportunity of reading an editorial in Meunier quebecois, which sums up the situation quite well, and I should like to onclude by quoting this article which, to my mind, reflects the opinion of the majority of Canadians.
The opinion expressed in the December 1973 issues of he Meunier quebecois concerning the chaotic situation resulting from the energy crisis is so pertinent that I shall quote a number of excerpts from it. Of course, I am still talking about Mr. Blanchard's article:
The great advantage of the present crisis is to make us realize how true federalism could function if it were really allowed to funtion fully and unreservedly to the benefit of all Canadians.
Oil and grains are both national products.
-for he was dealing both with agriculture and oil energy-
They are both treated with solicitude by the federal government which, with taxpayers' money, creates either a national oil corporation by investing $40 million as is presently the case, or a wheat board, as was the case in the past, again with money coming from all Canadians, and favoured by all federal services.
In all logic and fairness, these goods should be available to all Canadians at the same price, and mechanisms for equitable distribution should be provided through legislation. Otherwise how will it ever be possible, for instance, to reimburse eastern Canada for paying for western development and to compensate the Atlantic provinces for the artificial draining of industrial development willingly created by Ottawa policies?

The energy crisis will perhaps result in forcing central and western Canadians to think of all Canadians, to reconsider their economic philosophy, not in terms of a selfish and provincial development, but in terms of a planned and continental development.
A way was opened during the critical review of our grain policy which, while keeping eastern Canada as hostage, was annihilating eastern agriculture to the detriment of collective interests, especially consumers' interests.
Another avenue has just opened tearing away the Borden line that was devised to further benefit regional interests against the principles and practice of free trade between the provinces that are favourable to the development of a sound federalism. Through tearing into pieces a Canadian constitution that is soiled and torn by so many blows that reasons of state seem to justify, such as those that were struck according to Caesar's technique, will crises finally launch the country beyond its domestic disputes towards new horizons?
This is undoubtedly the dream of both smaller and greater Canadian citizens.

Mr. Speaker, the new time limits unfortunately make it difficult to observe the courtesies that are normally extended during this debate.

Nevertheless, I wish to pay tribute to the dignified representatives of the Queen, His Excellency the Governor General and his charming wife, and to offer them the best wishes of my constituents for a quiet and flourishing future in their new duties, as well as to wish them a pleasant journey in the riding of Esquimalt-Saanich where they are expected in early April.

Without further ado, Mr. Speaker, I will turn to the substance of my contribution to this debate. My concern today is with that class of persons virtually overlooked in the Speech from the Throne, the elderly, those living on fixed limited incomes. However, I do not intend to get into any auction to outbid other members or other parties by suggesting increased pension levels. Rather, my plan is to explore the few ideas the intent of which would be to contribute to the alleviation of their present worries, that is shortage of real income to bear the brunt of inflation and taxation.
I ask myself why, in their advanced years, they should have the problems of inflation and heavy taxation to deal with in addition to all their other problems such as, sickness possibly, oft times loneliness and frequently frustration at not being able to do as quickly the things they once did with such ease. We cannot disregard this part of our community. We are what we are because of the sacrifices they made for us. They do not expect sacrifices from us for them, but I say, why should we not do something for them even if it costs a sacrifice or two? We are an extremely fortunate generation, thanks in large part to their efforts. Let us not forget that.
If this land is strong, Mr. Speaker, the credit goes entirely to those from whom we inherited this land and our institutions. It is arrogance supreme to suggest otherwise.
I am hoping that out of the various proposals that I shall be making, one or two, individually or in combination, will prove acceptable to this government or its replacement after the next election, hopefully a Conservative government.
March 11, 1974

To set the scene in realism, I wish to read part of a letter that reached me only last week as I was preparing my remarks for this debate. It is a direct reflection on our performance as parliamentarians and, unfortunately, a well merited one. It confirms my decision that the line of my thinking is one I ought to take in this debate. The correspondence reads in part:
Those of us who began to buy our pensions fifty or sixty years ago, and who have been forced into retirement for the past fifteen or twenty years, find that our pensions plus the Old Age Security amount to little more than the Old Age Security plus the Supplement. We struggled to save money and we struggled to pay our taxes and are now no better off than those who saved nothing and, in many cases, paid no taxes either.
Now we still have to struggle to pay our little $300 or $400 income taxes...
I'm sure that you ... realize... the difficulties of those who find themselves on fixed incomes and pensions tied to pre-inflation levels.... I can only hope that my plea ... will cause you to raise your voice even louder than before.
This, Mr. Speaker, is a cri de coeur. There is something drastically wrong when citizens with the foresight to make provision for their declining years feel compelled to let out a cry like that. Having saved in their younger days, they do not begrudge the man who tries to save today. What they deplore is that they should have to go on paying in order to support those who are unwilling to save, or who are deriving benefits from social services which are available now but which were not available in their day. A balance must somehow be restored. The middle income group, about which I am speaking, is the source of much of the government's income tax revenue. These people are the backbone of our society, not only in numbers but in attitude. Let us not forget this. Those who can continue to find employment and who can secure adjustments in their wages may be able to shoulder the burden of rising costs and heavier taxation. Those who have retired and who are living on fixed incomes cannot. They must be relieved of at least part of the burden under which they labour.
This brings me to the proposal I wish to put forward. Thinking through these ideas I found it necessary to develop a dual concept involving an existence income level and a comfort income level-those terms could be defined without too much trouble; their names convey what is meant clearly enough. My purpose in introducing these notions is to suggest that those on pensions should be permitted a deduction level much higher than the present level of deductions for income tax purposes in order to achieve the comfort income level. I am referring to those on fixed incomes aged 65 or more.
The existence level is introduced for the same class of person. It is much lower than the comfort level, as its name implies, and is intended to be the deduction level for income tax purposes applicable to persons who are fortunate enough to enjoy incomes in excess of the comfort level. What I am endeavouring to do is to discriminate in favour of the provident. I have no built in objection to making discriminatory judgments; I am sure we all make judgments of this kind day after day. Indeed, I see every reason for making discriminatory judgments in this case. Certainly, there is no reason for penalizing anybody once
The Address-Mr. D. W. Munro the age of retirement has been reached, and preventing him from taking advantage of his providence. Further, in these improvident days there is something to be said in favour of encouraging providence. The notion that one needs to provide for one's own future is being discarded as outmoded. But it is not. It is one we should strive to maintain, and for this reason I suggest a revised income tax scale applicable to the elderly.
Next, I think of the widow or widower who suddenly finds that the family income has been halved through the death of a partner. Unfortunately, it is not only those who draw OAS benefits who find themselves in this plight. It occurs equally to those receiving superannuation benefits, not to mention those in receipt of disability pensions. Why should this be? What puzzles me is the way in which those who devise these schemes ignore the fact that a number of expenses continue unaffected-telephone bills, mortgage payments, light and heat, household repairs, and so on. In the case of contributive schemes why, I feel obliged to ask, should income be halved when the nominal contributor dies but remain untouched when the other spouse dies, the so-called non-contributor. There is real discrimination here. By my reckoning, the partners in any marr:age are contributors on an equal footing to any superannuation scheme they may have chosen.
As far as I am concerned, deductions from the pay cheque are deductions from the family income-the disposable family income is reduced by that amount. Why, then, should the wife, say, be deprived of half the pension just because the husband dies whereas, should the wife die, the husband's income continues unabated. This is discrimination on the basis of sex, if you like. I see that, according to the newspapers this morning, Ontario is thinking along these lines. High time we all did-but don't put me down as a women's liber for having said so. I am not. While we are on the subject of discrimination I might point out that the whole area of the pension rights of the housewife whether contributing or not, will have to be sorted out.
But let me get back to my main theme. I was asking how it came about that those who devised these various schemes failed to take into account continuing unaffected expenses. I had in mind the odd jobs around the house, like fixing a leaky tap or repairing an electrical connection or cutting a lawn. Such tasks now have to be paid for by a person living on half the pension which was formerly available. The method used in the treatment of widows and widowers also adversely affects persons receiving disability pensions. A friend of mine who was blinded during the war was awarded a disability pension on that account and received, as well, special pension assistance because his wife was an essential help to him. He lost that special pension assistance when his wife died. He even lost the monetary ability to hire daily help. And he was a blind man, at that. Who drew up these regulations which result in such hardship on occasion? Why do we not change them? So, I speak up for a more realistic and humanistic approach to the monetary consequences which flow from bereavement such as those consequences affecting income derived from annuities and pensions.
I also have in mind those whose income falls between my existence level and my comfort level and who are age

March 11, 1974
The Address-Mr. J. R. Gauthier
65 or over. I suggest they might be exempted from liability to pay municipal taxes on property. This may appear to be an invasion of the provincial revenue field, but my proposal goes further to suggest that any revenue which the municipalities might lose in consequence of such a remission would be made up by the federal authority, on application. This, again, is obviously a discriminatory benefit. Therefore, I would extend this tax advantage to those elderly people who are living in rented accommodation so that they would be exempted from the municipal tax portion of their rent.
I speak next of those who, in their earlier days, laid aside funds, as in our youth we were all taught to do, those who saved, and who now find that those savings are subject to a capital gains tax. They find that the time has come to use those savings either to meet a need, possibly because of high medical expenditures, or simply to enjoy a trip around the world. When they come to count their money they realize that part of it is subject to tax. Why should they now be denied, the full benefit of having put away a few thousand dollars? Do not trot out the argument about cheating succession duties. First of all, I am not talking so much about those who leave estates of a value which would attract succession duties. I am talking about those who have tucked $3,000 or $4,000 away for a second honeymoon splurge. I have in mind those below the comfort level. I insist that it should not be beyond the ingenuity of our tax collectors, if they are properly instructed and inspired, to set levels above which these advantages might not apply and below which they should.
Finally, I should like to elaborate briefly on a further benefit which, in my view, ought to be available to those of our elderly who, for one reason or another, choose not to take advantage of such pension schemes as old age security. Why should these people not be permitted, if they do not need these funds now, to arrange their deferment so they can be used later when they are in need or in want or, failing that, can be included in their estate when they die?
I have other notions, Mr. Speaker, but I see my time has elapsed.

Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to begin this new session by taking part in this debate. Let me, Mr. Speaker, reiterate my deep gratitude for the enormous work that this venerable House, under your presidency, has managed to accomplish during the first session. It is a considerable and positive achievement, considering the magnitude of the task that awaited us barely a year ago. That is something to be very proud of.
I join the hon. member for Spadina (Mr. Stollery) and the hon. member for Sherbrooke (Mr. Pelletier) in paying my tributes to His Excellency the Governor General and to Madame Leger. I represent, Mr. Speaker, the riding of Ottawa-Vanier where the vice-regal couple resides.
Needless to say, Mr. Speaker, how much I enjoyed my first year as a member. In the House of Commons, as elsewhere, it is very pleasant. I have met men and women with different cultural and professional backgrounds, but
(Mr. Munro (Esquimalt-Saanich).]
united by the same desire for objectivity, working and living an exceptional experience for the development of the Canadian society and the well-being of our people.
Therefore, I am immensely pleased with the tremendous work accomplished by the right hon. Prime Minister Trudeau's government.
Mr. Speaker, if I may, I would like to point out some of my pet projects which I intend to submit to the House this year.
One of them will be related to the creation of a school of higher studies in public administration. The objective is to guarantee the presence in the public service of people whose experience, competence and ability will designate as capable of fulfilling administrative duties, through democratic recruiting and a happy combination of knowledge and experience. A school of public administration would enable public servants to get further training, to specialize in the execution of their own duties, that is those of senior administrators.
The courses would also be offered to university graduates who want to pursue a career in the public service.
Today, training and development programs for federal public servants are partly within the jurisdiction of the Treasury Board and the Public Service Commission. We do of course send public servants to highly specialized institutions to complete their education. We are now sending some of them in Great Britain and France.
We also have agreements with Carleton and Ottawa universities for courses in public administration and management sciences. In addition we have the CAP program, which is the Career Assignment Program.
This study and training program, followed by on-the-job training periods, makes it possible for promising intermediate managers to develop their skills more rapidly and to accede later to senior managerial positions.
But this program is open to fewer than one hundred persons every year. Of course, many public servants will never have the opportunity to follow such accelerated courses, even if they have the required capabilities to apply for intermediate or senior managerial positions.
It is therefore important to consider seriously the creation of a bilingual school of higher studies in public administration.
If the government were interested in such a project, we could find here in Ottawa appropriate quarters where students could be given their theoretical and practical training, in the very heart of government activities. [English]
Since the hon. member for Grenville-Carleton (Mr. Baker) has once again demonstrated, as usual, his lack of knowledge concerning bilingualism, I should like now to address myself to this most important question of bilingualism.
I, too, have the honour of representing in the House many citizens employed as public servants, by crown corporations and agencies. Members of the armed forces of Canada as well as their families who reside in my riding. The hon. member for Grenville-Carleton has implied that civil servants in his riding are critical of and impatient with the process of identification and designation of posi-
March 11, 1974

tions for the purpose of implementing the bilingualism policy of this parliament.
In essence, in his speech on March 8, 1974, the hon. member for Grenville-Carleton said that he has received more mail and more telephone calls on this question than on any other subject. As reported at page 342 of Hansard. for March 8 the hon. member said:
From the tone of these letters and telephone calls it is alarmingly evident that the difficulty of implementation of a policy of unilingual-ism in the public service that was to be overcome by the guidelines approved by parliament has in fact become more intense and as a result I believe the morale of the public service is being seriously undermined. I say to you, Mr. Speaker, that the service is being damaged as a result.
By virtue of this statement the hon. member for Grenville-Carleton is again demonstrating his lack of understanding of the fundamentals of bilingualism. As the Ottawa Journal stated in their lead editorial of February 20, 1974:
Neither Grenville-Carleton MP Walter Baker nor anyone else is able at this time to say whether 50,000 bilingual positions out of some 260,000 positions in the public service are too many or too few. It is unfortunate that Mr. Baker rushed in so quickly with his intemperate criticism. His impetuosity and his apparent failure to recognize all the reasons for bilingualism call into question once more his commitment to the Official Languages Act beyond lip-service and mere tokenism.
Such an attitude may be understandable, even excusable in MPs from out of the way places; it is not to be condoned in any MP - from any part - representing a constituency in the National Capital region. Mr. Baker has yet to achieve the breadth of vision on this subject of his leader, Robert Stanfield.
I agree with the Ottawa Journal that the hon. member for Grenville-Carleton is only paying lip-service and giving mere tokenism to bilingualism, and by so doing he is rendering a disservice to Canada and Canadians.
To further demonstrate his lack of understanding, he stated, as reported on page 342 of Hansard:
The 1976 deadline was established for an estimate of 25,000 bilingual positions.
It has been stated time and time again by the President of the Treasury Board (Mr. Drury) that the target date aimed at is 1978, not 1976. This is evidence again of his lack of understanding of bilingualism and, more importantly, its implementation as it affects the public service.
In the interest of truth and accuracy, I want to make it clear that the target date for designation of bilingual positions within the public service is 1978 and that it never was 1976. The hon. member for Grenville-Carleton also stated on the CTV network on Saturday last that the target date was 1976, and this, as I have stated, is not true. It is now very apparent that the hon. member for Gren-ville-Carleton's avowed policy of unilingualism in the civil service and, in the words of the Ottawa Journal, "his apparent failure to recognize all the reasons for bilingualism" call into question once more his commitment to the Official Languages Act beyond lipservice and mere tokenism. That, coupled with his inexcusable ignorance of the target date with respect to implementation and designation, indicates quite clearly that this House and the general public have been misled, not through dishonesty but through his ignorance of the facts.
This attitude does not surprise me. It is witness to his real intention and possible thoughts on this whole ques-
The Address-Mr. J. R. Gauthier tion, and it supports the position some of his colleagues in this House have expressed frequently. These ardent supporters of the status quo have been crying and moaning about things bilingual for the last six years. It is always, in their view, being implemented too fast, too much, too costly. The only avowed policy some Conservative members seem to extol regarding bilingualism is to give lip support to the principle, but by all means slow down and stop the implementation of this important and vital national policy.

speakerposition: Deputy Whip of the Progressive Conservative Party
speechtext: That is not true.

That is what you say. Rather than help in the difficult task of achieving the effective implementation of institutional bilingualism, some members of the Official Opposition cultivate the fear psychosis, and suggest that whatever is done is always too fast, too costly and too much. As a matter of fact, some members in the opposition have become the moral guarantors for every bigot across this country who quotes them and uses them to destroy rather than to build this Canada of ours. At this time no one would deny that the working language in inter-departmental exchanges is English. I do not dispute this fact. No one can read anything into the present law in respect of such exchanges. Neither this parliament, the staff associations nor public servants are advocating a policy of unilingualism, and I suggest that the hon. member for Grenville-Carleton is retrograde in this approach.
Many bilingual Francophones have come to work and have had to work in the English language, not because of preference but because of necessity. In a document filed by the Public Service Commission it is stated that in 1971, for example, of the 88,484 public service appointments in that year 21.4 per cent claimed French as their working language, yet only 11 per cent were appointed to positions requiring this language. In subsequent years, 1972 and 1973, the same report stated that an increased percentage of Canadians working in the Public Service are able to work, if they so desire and are needed, in the official language of their choice. It is only fair to say that if anybody should be pressuring and showing their impatience it is the thousands of bilingual civil servants who have been working in their second language, or the unilingual French, for that matter, who have had little chance of making a career in the public service.
The resolution adopted by parliament last year is not a threat to job security or promotion; it is a reasonable plan for equilibrium and equality. Nobody is born bilingual; he or she must be trained. This government is making a determined and commendable effort to promote institutional and individual bilingualism through training and understanding. The Official Languages Act and the program of bilingualism in the federal public service simply recognizes the realities of Canada as it is today.
The real solution lies in our educational system. This government has, for this obvious reason and also because of the previous unproductive system of teaching a second language in our schools, encouraged language training, and has dispensed in the last five years $300 million to our provinces. These special educational grants were for the

March 11, 1974
The Address-Mr. J. R. Gauthier purpose of improving and extending second-language training. Was this too much, too fast and too costly? I suggest that only the results will tell us that. In the Ottawa metropolitan area alone the Secretary of State (Mr. Faulkner) in 1973 added another $2 million a year for two years to finance an experimental program of new methods of teaching French to our English-speaking students. Provincial authorities should take up this program, particularly because of its importance in the Ottawa capital. Has this been too much, too fast and too costly? I suggest it has been quite the contrary.
Attitudes on bilingualism are changing and have changed. Bilingualism never meant, be it institutional or individual, that all Canadians should become bilingual. The capital of this country should rightly reflect the Canadian reality and, to the credit of the Ottawa and Carleton school boards, they are offering better courses in second-language training through government assistance to provincial education programs. I hope and pray that with understanding and love this issue of bilingualism will be better understood. Progress is apparent, and this is for the betterment and the unification of our country.

As a tangible example of understanding as to real bilingualism, I should like to deal now with my constituency and especially the city of Vanier.
Bill C-232 changed the name of my constituency of Ottawa East to that of Ottawa-Vanier. The purpose of such a change was certainly to promote further the bilingual identity of my constituency and more expecially to identify the city of Vanier as an integral part of our beautiful national capital. Under the able leadership of a far-sighted municipal government, the city of Vanier now has a master development plan. The recent decision to build the Vanier thoroughfare as a driveway rather than as a speedway, will contribute to the achievement of a road network through an economic commercial center, that will take into account the aesthetic aspect as well as the quality of life that citizens of that municipality wish to preserve. On account of its geographical situation, east of Ottawa's development centres, Vanier could not benefit from a swift and striking commercial expansion as some other sectors of our national capital.
Often forgotten as regards federal building projects, Vanier with its 23,000 citizens should hold the attention of federal planners when it comes to finding sites for public buildings. The National Capital Commission was created to draft plans for the development and improvement of the national capital area and should help Vanier so that the nature and character of the Canadian government centre may be in accordance with its national importance.
At the dawn of its new development, the city of Vanier should get from government agencies, such as the Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation, the National Capital Commission and the Department of Public Works, assistance for preserving, restoring and improving that fair municipality.

Mr. Speaker, before getting into my remarks on the Speech from the Throne I should like to congratulate the hon. members for Spadina (Mr. Stollery) and Sherbrooke (Mr. Pelletier) for their excellent presentations. Those two gentlemen talked in glowing terms about some country where all of the manifest problems of poverty, regional disparity, unemployment and all the other human problems had been solved by some supergovernment. I am afraid I did not catch the name of the country they were describing, but I assume it must have been Utopia, or perhaps Shangri La. They certainly could not have been talking about Canada, as anyone who can see, read and hear knows that those problems exist in Canada in abundance. In fact, they happen to be the most abundant commodities we have.
At page 12 of Hansard for February 27, the hon. member for Sherbrooke is reported as stating:
-the wealthiest country in the world, spending huge amounts, did not succeed in eliminating poverty.
I thought the hon. member was talking about this country and this government, but it turned out that he was speaking of the United States.
I do not know of a country in the world that has more resources, more unused manpower, more potential or more ingenuity when compared to our population than does our own country of Canada. Why then do we have so many people living in our bountiful society at or below the poverty line? Why do we have so many unemployed? Why
March 11, 1974

do we allow inflation to run unchecked, eroding the buying power of millions of families that have to provide shelter, food and clothing for themselves and their children?
I was intrigued by the statement of the hon. member for Sherbrooke that the United States had spent huge sums of money, but had failed to eliminate poverty from that country. I wonder what the hon. member thinks his colleagues on that side of the House have been doing for the past six years. We all know they have been spending money as if it were going out of style. And I will tell the hon. members across the floor that they have failed, utterly and completely, to eliminate poverty from this country. They have failed to eliminate regional disparities, and they have failed to provide jobs for the people in our country who want to work. What they have succeeded in doing has been to destroy the work ethic, divide our country into regional blocs, and to destroy the efficiency of the public service.
I suggest to members across the floor that they might as well not close and lock the door to the public treasury. The cupboard must be pretty bare by now. Right now the government is spending money that we do not have, and that leads me to believe that there is not any more left in the treasury. Last year, for instance, the gross public debt was $51.8 billion and the net national debt represented about $1,000 for every man, woman and child in Canada. I do not know yet what it is for the fiscal year ending March 31, 1974, but it must be in the area of $55 billion. We do know from the estimates, though, that it will cost $2.9 billions this year just to service the national debt. That is money we cannot spend on services or benefits because, in effect, it has already been spent. This is money down the drain. That takes care of Shangri La and Utopia, Mr. Speaker. It is a very sad awakening, but it is reality, and I say to the government members, and especially to the cabinet members who are squandering our money, stop building castles in the sky; stop living in a dream world and come down here and face reality.
The problems we had when the present government took over are still with us. In fact, they are even worse now, and there are some new ones. There are new problems that have resulted from over-spending, inefficiency and just plain bungling. Those problems will not just disappear. They must be dealt with. But first, Mr. Speaker, the government will have to face up squarely to those problems, instead of trying to smother them with borrowed money.
I see that, according to the estimates, the government intends to create a few more agencies and corporations, possibly even some departments. This is scandalous, Mr. Speaker, but I have to admit that it is typical of the way the present government operates. If a department or agency is not able to cope with a given situation, create a new agency alongside the old, and transfer the responsibilities to the new one. Then you have two or three agencies fumbling with the same problems. We have more agencies and departments in our government than any other country in the western world and more cabinet ministers. We have more ministers in our federal cabinet than either the United States or Great Britain, and yet we
The Address-Mr. D. M. Beattie do not seem to be able to get a clear answer from the cabinet on even the most simple and clear-cut issues.
There are 47 members of the government caucus who are either ministers or parliamentary secretaries, almost 50 per cent of the entire caucus. I can't help thinking there must be an awful lot of jockeying over there for positions of power, and the authority to spend those billions of dollars in the estimates. It is easy to understand why they seem to have so much trouble making decisions on even the most vital issues facing the country. It is abundantly clear by now that whatever it is they are doing, they are doing very much for the Canadian people. It is time they started looking after the business of running the country. The present government has more than doubled the national budget in only six years, and I do not think it is too much to expect the government to start showing some results for all that money.
The Unemployment Insurance Commission is in a scandalous mess and, in fact, the whole system of social services in Canada today is in a mess. Who would have imagined just six years ago that the cost of the UIC would rise to more than $2 billion by the year 1973? And that seems to be only the beginning. UIC is already showing signs of surpassing that figure in the coming year, and still the government refuses to undertake a full inquiry of the program, and of the department that is administering the program. This is a very vital program, Mr. Speaker. It was designed to provide assistance to people in the work force who, for a variety of reasons, might find themselves unemployed. Every member of this House accepts the UIC, and the concept behind it, as a responsibility of the government. It is not the UIC to which we in the official opposition are objecting. It is the administration that we quarrel with, and for very good reasons.
The Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Stanfield) has called for an inquiry into the operation of the UIC, stating that the agency has been operating under a cloud of suspicion for a very long time, and that it is time to clear the air. I agree with that wholeheartedly, and I would add that if we undertake an investigation into the administration of UIC, a lot of heads will roll. It should be obvious to anyone that a large percentage of the two billion dollars spent last year on UIC went to sources other than the legitimate claimants who had paid premiums into the program. An overhaul of UIC would give us an opportunity to do something else very important. It would allow us to restructure the whole manpower-UIC set-up. We would be able to develop programs whereby people could be trained for the jobs that exist, jobs that cannot presently be filled from the labour pool. Advances in technology have passed tens of thousands of people by, leaving them in a situation where they would like to work but cannot qualify for the jobs that are offered them.
I get letters from leaders in industry pointing out difficulties faced by employers in filling job vacancies. Many industries just cannot afford to train prospective employees. In many other cases people are trained for jobs and, after they have worked for the minimum period required to qualify for UIC benefits, they contrive to get themselves fired or just quit, forcing the employer to go through the training process all over again. Other employers have told me that people who are receiving unemploy-

March 11, 1974
The Address-Mr. D. M. Beattie
ment benefits will conduct themselves in job interviews in such a way as to discourage employers from hiring them. In spite of the fact that the present government appears to be bent on destroying the traditional Canadian work ethic, I am convinced that the vast majority of Canadians want to work. They want to work at jobs that pay a living wage, jobs that have some promise of advancement and jobs that are not deadends in themselves. The provision of such jobs is not an impossible task for government. We have the human and natural resources; we have the ingenuity and, most of all, we have the responsibility to provide incentives and opportunities.
I should mention here that every time the government gets caught in an obvious blunder or boondoggle, which happens with tiresome regularity, the minister involved in the blunder tries to place the blame at the feet of the official opposition. Each time they try to do so, it is so obvious that it is often amusing. For instance, in the case of Bill C-125, the minister responsible for the UIC has been saying lately that it was the official opposition that prevented it from being tabled for debate in the House. Bill C-125 would have brought about some needed changes in the administration of UIC, something we in the official opposition have been urging the government to do for the past two or three years. The minister neglected to note that Bill C-125 was a government bill, and that after it had passed first reading it was put on the shelf. The government did not have to worry about the NDP on Bill C-125. The NDP will go along with anything. The government did not have to worry about the Conservative opposition. We were the ones who asked for the bill. No, Mr. Speaker, the minister was worried about his own causus. It was the Libera, caucus that was divided on C-125, and it would have proven embarrassing to the government to have its own members oppose efforts to clean up the mess in the UIC. I predict this failure will come back to haunt them some day soon.
Mr. Speaker, there is another example of bungling that deserves some mention, and that is the matter of the CRTC advertising in newspapers around the country. I have noticed that the CRTC places ads in French in English-language newspapers and in English in French-language newspapers. I ask my colleagues to think about this, Mr. Speaker. A person who does not speak French is asked to read and comprehend an advertisement in the French language. And, in Quebec, a person who does not understand English is asked by CRTC to read and comprehend an advertisement in the English language. This, in my opinion, is a useless waste of the taxpayers money. Unfortunately, that is not an isolated incident. There are indications that in some departments that sort of thing is the norm, and I doubt that the people responsible are aware of just how ludicrous it is. It certainly could not be in the interest of national unity. This sort of thing has the opposite effect. It tends to agitate and alienate people, and too much of that is being done already as witnessed by the remarks of the previous speaker.
I have been speaking out publicly for some time about the way our immigration laws are being administered, and in particular I have been drawing attention to the way foreign students are allowed to enter our country without

proper screening and without follow up supervision. People who would not otherwise qualify for landed immigrants status are flooding into the country under cover of our lax foreign student programs, and some of these people are being aided and abetted by corrupt immigration officials. Some of these officials have already been uncovered, but it is highly unlikely that they will all be found out unless a full inquiry is undertaken.
Equally important is the matter of how many so-called students are living underground throughout the country with false documents or without documents of any kind. Those who have papers can get by for an indefinite time unless they are sought out and deported. Those who do not have documentation are at the mercy of unscrupulous employers and underworld figures. A few months ago we had a period of amnesty during which people living here illegally could come forward without fear of prosecution. This was considered to be cheaper than searching them out, and naturally it would have to be considered more humane. What this has done in fact has been to make us out to be a bunch of patsies as far as our immigration laws are concerned. We are the world's greatest pushovers for people who cannot qualify to enter and become citizens of countries with realistic immigration laws. The amnesty period last year was not exactly a success as far as bringing illegal residents out of hiding is concerned. The minister in charge of immigration admitted that only a small percentage of suspected illegal entrants actually came forward and that there are probably many thousands of them still living here underground. Since that time people have been pouring into the country, taking advantage of loopholes in the laws.
The question I ask now is not whether there will be another amnesty, but when. This raises another question, and that is just who is a refugee so far as our immigration laws are concerned. We have established what the government calls "an immigration presence" in Chile to handle applications from Chilean refugees, and the Minister of Manpower and Immigration (Mr. Andras) said that these immigration officers will remain in Chile until at least the end of this year to handle an ongoing refugee program. Is there some magic formula for deciding who is a bona fide refugee, or is it only necessary for a person to sidle up to a Canadian immigration officer and say: "I am a Marxist terrorist and the present government in Chile won't let me engage in subversive activities"? I suggest that is something like the situation because if these people are in so little danger that they can wait for months or a year to be granted paid passage to Canada, then there is something fishy about this whole question of giving refugee status. According to figures released by the immigration department, only a small percentage of ordinary immigration applicants are approved in Chile at present while a very large percentage of refugee applicants are approved.
Our immigration laws are designed to give protection to those people who have a legal right to live in our country, and they are designed to protect our system from those who would come here and plot to tear down everything that we have worked so hard to build. At present these laws do not protect us. They protect the very people whom we should be turning away at our borders. If our immigration laws are too lax, then let us tighten them up. If our laws are adequate and the fault lies with the administra-

tion of the law, then let us root out those who are delinquent. I suggest that there is ample reason to undertake an inquiry into the whole immigration machinery and find out where the fault lies.
In conclusion, Mr. Speaker-

Mr. Speaker, exactly 14 months ago, I gave my first speech in the House during the debate on last year's Speech from the Throne. At that time I outlined the five guidelines established by the government as a basis for a comprehensive review of the Canadian social security system, and I indicated the formulas that we had considered for implementing these policy statements.
From the start, we recognized that if such a re-organization of all the social policies of Canada were to become reality and meet its anticipated objectives, we had to obtain the commitment and active participation of all the provinces. Indeed, this is why the working paper on social security in Canada was tabled in the House of Commons in April 1973. In a way, this was the contribution of the federal government to the initial steps of the reform.
The working paper outlined five strategic schemes which appeared appropriate for us to follow with a view to achieving a model of social system. They were supported by 14 proposals which seemed likely to facilitate the implementation of those schemes.
In April 1973, the first of a series of meetings which were to follow brought the welfare ministers together in Ottawa. Moreover, it was with that federal-provincial conference that was officially launched the joint federal-provincial review of the social security system in Canada. Indeed, after having looked into the working paper, the provinces recognized by common agreement that the schemes and the proposals as outlined in the working paper could certainly serve as the starting point and as terms of reference all along the review work.

Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to report that as a result of the leadership of this Liberal government and the hard work of both federal and provincial governments, the joint federal-provincial review group has made excellent progress over the past year. Significant improvements have
The Address-Mr. Lalonde
already been made in a number of federal and provincial social security programs.
First, in July we introduced a new Family Allowances Act which tripled the average allowances for children starting in January of this year. We provided that these benefits would be automatically escalated each year in line with increases in the cost of living to enable Canada's low and middle income families better to meet the increased costs of raising children. Moreover, in order to protect the purchasing power of Canadian families in the face of a rapid worldwide inflation, the government acted swiftly in September to increase family allowance benefits as an interim measure until the proposed increases were effected in January.
The ability of the provinces to adjust family allowance payments to meet the particular needs of their people reflects a new approach to the integration of the social security system in each province under which there is greater provincial flexibility and, at the same time, better co-ordination of federal and provincial elements of the social security system. I suggest that this is a significant step in resolving the deep federal-provincial differences which had developed over how responsibility for social security measures should be divided between the federal government and the provinces, and I suggest again that this is truly a remarkable achievement for federalism.
Second, in April, 1973, old age security pensions were substantially increased. Also, in October we shifted from an annual to a quarterly basis for escalation of both old age security pensions and the guaranteed income supplement to ensure that these benefits keep pace with increases in the cost of living. We have raised the combined pension and supplement from $150 per month in March, 1973 to $187 per month in April, 1974.
Third, in October we introduced changes in the Canada Pension Plan to increase the earnings ceiling for the years 1974 and 1975 and to remove the 2 per cent ceiling on the annual escalation of pension benefits, so that in future benefits would rise in line with the full increase in the cost of living. In addition, the full purchasing power of benefits already in pay on December 31, 1973, was restored.
With these changes, the federal government and the provinces have, in a matter of months, taken together a major step toward harmonizing the Canada and Quebec pension plans. It is a tribute to federal-provincial co-operation as it can be practised, and represents the way this government approaches federal-provincial relations. Furthermore, the government has provided for the automatic escalation of virtually all federal programs, in accordance with increases in the cost of living. I am thinking here particularly of benefits to veterans and the superannuation pensions of federal public servants.
Mr. Speaker, the recent Speech from the Throne has already indicated a number of areas in which we hope to take action this year in order to further improve our social security system. In the very near future I plan to introduce further amendments to the Canada Pension Plan that have been worked out in conjunction with the provincial governments. These amendments will provide for a new formula that will tie the earnings ceiling on

March 11, 1974
The Address-Mr. Lalonde
which pension benefits are based each year to an earnings index, the average level of wages and salaries for the year. They will provide for the elimination of the earnings test now in effect for people aged 65 to 69. Such people will then be able to apply for and receive their full Canada Pension Plan retirement benefit without having it reduced to take account of earnings from employment. It is estimated that approximately 35,000 persons, who are at present receiving no pension or only a partial one, will directly benefit from this measure. This removes a discriminatory feature against those persons who work to supplement their pensions because the earnings test only applies to earnings from employment and not from other sources, such as investment.
There will also be an amendment that will ensure equality of treatment for male and female contributors to the Canada Pension Plan. As the government indicated in the Speech from the Throne, this latter change is but one of several measures this government plans to take to improve the status of women in Canada.

As to the review of the social security system, the ministers concentrate all their efforts on two specific objectives: first, we must formulate a satisfying concept for an income supplement plan and, second, prepare an efficient collective employment policy.
In view of the enormous and complex task we are undertaking, my provincial counterparts and I do not expect to be able to be through discussing these questions before the end of 1974 or the beginning of 1975.
But there is a statement I wish to make today on a specific question, a specific service, that is daycare services.

The government has placed a high priority on daycare services where there is a social need for such services. This is in keeping with the government's objective of removing barriers to entry to the regular labour market. There is a definite trend whereby married women are entering and re-entering the labour market at all levels. In 1962, there were 870,000 married women in the labour force with a participation rate of 21.6 per cent; in 1970, there were 1.7 million married women in the labour force with a participation rate of nearly 34 per cent. In 1972, the participation rate of women aged 25 to 64 was 40 per cent but the participation rate of young married women aged 20 to 24 was even higher, at 47.4 per cent.
The need for day care services has also been amply demonstrated by the number of LIP projects in this respect. The government recognizes that this need is a continuous one and will make special efforts on a continuing basis to aid those mothers with young children in their care who seek employment but who also want to ensure that their children are properly supervised.
I would remind the House what this government is already doing in this area. As a result of amendments to the Canada Assistance Plan Regulations in 1972, shareable costs for day care services are the full operating costs, including costs of equipment and supplies and rent or depreciation on capital. For all other welfare services, shareable costs are restricted to salaries and related staff

costs. The increased cost sharing has given considerable impetus to the development of day care services.
The Canadian Council on Social Development has been given a grant to develop national norms for the development of day care services for children, in collaboration with officials of my department. In addition, consultative services are provided by my department to provinces, municipalities, voluntary agencies and community groups. Hon. members will also recall that the government established in 1972 an information centre on day care. This information centre has proven very efficient and very useful all across the land.
If day care centres are seen by a community as essential facilities to enable mothers with small children to become self-supporting, then we believe we should help to provide such services. Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to be able to announce today our new position on cost-sharing with the provinces of day care services for low and below average income families. The government has approved new policy guidelines for day care services shareable under the Canada Assistance Plan. These guidelines are designed to ensure that federal sharing is available to low and below average income families who need day care services. Priority is given to single parent families, families with health and social problems, working mothers and handicapped children. The guidelines provide for income tested programs in line with the recommendations of the Royal Commission on the Status of Women. Several provinces have already initiated steps in this direction, and several other provinces have given evidence of being interested in the development of similar programs.
In summary, Mr. Speaker, since the social security review was launched we have increased family allowances substantially, provided for greater flexibility in meeting provincial social priorities through variations in family allowances, revised the Canada Pension Plan to bring the ceiling on pensionable earnings closer in line with average wages, provided for the automatic escalation of all federal pensions and allowances on an annual or in some cases a quarterly basis and have taken steps to improve the arrangements under the Canada Assistance Plan for sharing in the costs of day care services provided by the provinces to low and below average income families, and especially to heads of single parent families. All these major steps we have taken during the ten short months that the review has been under way.
Because of the spirit of co-operation evidenced in the federal-provincial conferences and because of the support, encouragement and suggestions received from scores of voluntary organizations, labour unions, trade associations and religious groups, the government is confident that the social security review can be completed by the target date of April, 1975, and that the agreed upon changes can be implemented over the three to five year period which began in April, 1973.
I would like to conclude these remarks, Mr. Speaker, by setting the record straight concerning my department's share of the increase in the budget for next year. There have been several articles recently on this matter and I must admit that I am never surprised, although I am sometimes dismayed with press headlines and editorials, admittedly in the minority, which on the one hand call for
March 11, 1974

concrete steps by governments to solve various social problems and then complain when solutions result in increased government spending. They make me think of the double talk that we hear from the official opposition in this respect.
The proposed increase of $2.4 billion in the budget for next year over this year's forecast includes approximately $1.2 billion for the Department of National Health and Welfare. The real winners of this increase are the low and middle income Canadians and their families who have seen family allowances tripled, retired Canadians who have had their old age pensions benefits increased by over 32 per cent in one year and the provincial social assistance recipients, since federal spending in this area will increase by some $79 million, an increase of some 14 per cent in a single year.
Hear, hear!

Mr. Speaker, I rise to place on the record my comments on the throne speech. It is clear that at this time we are facing more uncertainty in the world than we have ever experienced since the end of the war. We see that the unprecedented rise in prosperity and affluence of the western world since the end of the war has been brought to a jarring halt. For many countries, this year will be a year of zero growth, or even of reduced growth. The United States is now in its second quarter of zero growth. Britain, it is forecast, will experience negative growth and Japanese growth is forecast at the low level of only 3 per cent.
For underdeveloped countries the situation is even worse. With regard to those countries, the increased cost of oil will make their economies much less productive and will prevent the modest increase that would have kept pace with the expansions of their populations. All this points to the fact that much of our affluence and production in society has been the result of the very low prices of energy, in the form of oil and gas. All the price increases of oil and gas really reflect the upward trend of basic commodity prices, which have not materially changed in 25 years. The price of wheat at $2 per bushel was reaching such a low level that production was being discouraged. This was the case with wool and other basic commodities. Yet, the price of manufactured goods and wages in general had risen markedly over the years. As this problem relating to the pricing of oil and gas is going to be very much to the fore in this parliament, we should realize that it is only part of the much larger problem of world supply of oil and gas.
It seems doubtful, Mr. Speaker, if the course being followed by the government in dealing with the producing
The Address-Mr. Ritchie
provinces, Alberta and Saskatchewan, is the best way to deal with the question of oil and gas. The government's approach will certainly leave scars on Canadian confederation long after the problem itself has been forgotten. Eventually, it will probably mean the drift of western Canada into an extremely independent position. Demand for energy is increasing all over the world. As the supply is decreasing, the price will go up regardless of what we, as politicians, say. In the handling of this problem it is important that we do not jeopardize supply for the future and bring about future shortages in our attempts to bring about short-term solutions.
Indeed, we are following, in many ways, the very course which the United States followed 20 years ago when it took a number of negative steps which, as a consequence, created its energy shortages of the present time. In the United States, price restraints were placed on producers, under the guise of providing assistance to consumers.
