It is painfully evident that, in the end, this was a great disservice to the consumer. The incentive for producers to explore was taken away; the finding rate fell drastically and reserve additions did not keep pace with consumption. The United States has now taken off price restraints and is allowing the competitive market system to set prices with regard to new supplies. In the final analysis, this will assist the consumer, as there is not much point in cheap oil if there is no oil to be had at any price.
In the United States, record expansion dollars are flowing back to help find much needed energy. We, in Canada, however, are largely following the pattern of the American administration of 20 years ago. We are more interested in the price of oil being low than in assuring the supply of oil and gas in future. It would appear, from many sources, it is generally believed that in western Canada there is an unlimited amount of oil to be scooped up for the taking. Such, however, does not seem to be the case. We are presently, and have been for some years, taking out of the ground half a billion barrels of oil more per year than are being found. Frontier oil may be very attractive in principle, but it is going to be terribly expensive by the time it reaches our consuming public.
It has always been assumed that the Alberta tar sands would be a source of cheap oil. It now seems abundantly clear that oil from the Alberta tar sands will be very expensive, but it will be useful in acting as a ceiling on what the Arab nations might demand for their oil. A comparison of relative costs of drilling and procuring oil from the tar sands indicates that recovery costs from conventional oil wells, in particular from ones as good as the Arab states now have, will be a governing factor in world oil prices for the balance of this decade or even this century.
An examination of statistics relating to relative costs of oil from the two sources is interesting. It has been estimated that it takes $10,000 of capital investment to extract one barrel of oil per day from the Alberta tar sands. Conversely, it takes $2,000 of investment in conventional oil wells in continental North America, including Alberta, to produce one barrel per day. But, for the Arab states, it takes an investment of only a few hundred dollars for a well that will produce one barrel per day. A good well in North America is rated at 50 barrels per day, whereas in the Arab

March 11, 1974
The Address-Mr. Ritchie
countries a production rate of 5,000 barrels per day is quite average.
Then, again, the Alberta tar sands product involves a mining operation rather than drilling for a conventional oil well. The exploitation of the tar sands will require a lot of manpower, which will be highly unionized. Workers will demand high and steadily increasing wages as their rightful due. In the case of oil wells, on the other hand, once they are brought into production, the labour content is not high. So, it is not difficult to see how the Arab nations will control price in future. We must also bear in mind, however, that the price of oil on the markets of the world seems to be declining. It is now forecast that about $8 per barrel will be the new price.
The United States President has told his nation of the measures to be taken to handle the serious American oil shortage which has been caused by the Arab denial of petroleum, and of other measures which will be necessary if the Arab squeeze continues. He has stated that by the end of this decade his country will have developed the potential to meet its energy needs without dependence on any foreign nation. The President did not make any reference to any nation as being an exception. The Americans have talked about the continental concept under which Canada and the United States would work together. It now seems likely that the United States has reversed its attitude with regard to Canada.
As late as in 1969, the United States Cabinet report on energy futures recommended close relations with Canada on energy, but suggested that Canada could only be counted on as a secure source of oil and gas if Canada took steps to reduce the dependence of Quebec and the Maritimes on overseas imports. Ottawa rejected this plan. Later on, with regard to the possibility of Prudoe Bay oil being brought by the Mackenzie Valley pipeline, Ottawa declined to put the matter on the agenda for intercabinet discussion, on the grounds that Ottawa had not set up its own policy and, of course, the United States plumped for the TransAlaska oil pipeline. At the present time it also seems likely that the Prudhoe Bay Gas will also go by Alaska, as the Americans have indicated they are in favour of an Alaskan pipeline.
One cannot blame the Americans for their sharp change in official and public attitudes when, without consultation, Ottawa slapped on the export tax in September. The situation was made even worse when the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. Macdonald) stated that he would cut petroleum exports to the United States if the Arabs demanded it.
These were Ottawa's actions against the United States, whose oil saved Canada from the long energy crisis in World War II and whose oil fields sustained Canadian growth, including that of western Canada, up to the midfifties. The United States has provided three quarters of the oil market growth for western Canadian oil for the past decade and thus made possible the productive capacity of the Alberta oil fields today. In view of the present huge trade between the two countries being balanced heavily in Canada's favour it is quite possible and likely that retaliation on the part of the United States will occur.
The federal-provincial energy conference is over. It adjourned with Canada being still no closer to a national

energy policy, although all the provinces had shown their positions before the conference. Ottawa had remained quiet. In view of the proposal that the price of crude oil be raised to $6 per barrel, that $1 per barrel go to the eastern consumer, 56 cents to the oil producing provinces, 33 cents to industry and 13 cents to the federal government, it was obvious that there was not enough money to satisfy all. In the long term, after the restraint period, there was to be an agreed increase in price. The Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce (Mr. Gillespie) suggested that, somehow, we could insulate ourselves from the world. There was to be one price across the country.
The Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) said the other day that he was not interested in confiscating any province's resources. Nevertheless, the oil export tax cannot be construed as anything but the confiscation of a province's resources, in its present form. The charge made that the export tax was necessary to prevent so-called windfall profits, is not exactly true. Most of the extra money would still have found its way to the federal or provincial treasuries. But, if there are to be windfall profits, one sees the importance of having in place an excess profits tax which should be applied in all circumstances, and not just to the oil industry. It should apply to all industries which show a very high profit ratio.
The recent move by President Nixon with regard to the 22 per cent depletion allowance-that allowance, now granted to U.S. companies in foreign countries, would be eliminated-means that Canada would lose a certain amount of money that would have come from U.S. investment in Canada. That means that Canadian institutions and individual Canadians will need to make up this loss out of their savings.
The social security program in place in Canada, as announced and elaborated on by the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Lalonde) makes savings by ordinary, individual Canadians almost superfluous. As the rapid rise in inflation largely eats up these savings, one wonders for how long Canadians will be foolish enough to invest. Western Canada was founded by many races, but had in common the symbolism of the British connection. However, the British connection is diminishing in its force, prodded and abetted by Ottawa, and the new symbols of central Canada found little acceptance in the western mind. The maple leaf is an example because many western Canadians have never seen an actual maple leaf.
A legal and constitutional battle, by which this federal government intends to lay the provinces low, is intended, in view of the apparent packing of the supreme court by the appointment of certain justices recently. Chief Justice Laskin is noted as being left of centre and a strong federalist. Then there was the appointment of Jean Baetz, the former constitutional adviser to the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau). At the opening of the University of Saskatchewan law school in 1965, the Chief Justice made the statement, and I quote:
Power contracts by a failure to use it.
March 11, 1974

He later said:
I borrow a phrase from my friend, Professor Frank Scott. Provincial autonomy means national inactivity, and I would add that the more we have of the one, the more we have of the other...
I find it difficult to believe that our federal system can endure unless Ottawa is accepted as a source of national power and authority exercisable in respect of and for all citizens of Canada.
In view of that statement, it is not to be wondered that the president of the Law Society of Alberta called the appointment of Laskin as Chief Justice an overt political act. Has the Prime Minister decided to pack the court? By so doing, does he hope the federal government will usurp the power of the provinces? Can provincial jurisdictions expect to have a reasonable hearing in a packed supreme court? Western Canada has come of age in its political thinking. Its resources and its people give it new impetus and a new direction. It is more confident that it is equal to the rest of the Canadian confederation. It is confident that it can stand on its own if it needs to do so. It does not wish to be a hewer of wood and a drawer of water for central Canada. It doubts that the excessive reliance on prohibiting the export of resources and products, except in the processed form, will be enough to sustain the Canadian economy at the level that it wishes. The manufacturing industry is hard put in Canada to maintain its job numbers and its only major market, the United States, will find it increasingly difficult to absorb its high price products.
Mr. Speaker, it is very fashionable to blame oil companies and other large companies for rip-offs and so on which the leader of the NDP seems to favour as his attack on the bad guys. In deference to him, no doubt, the Prime Minister suggested that his government would also be after the bad guys, the oil companies, if they charged too much. However, Mr. Speaker, it should be realized that a corporation is not a person in itself. The implication of these attacks is that profits benefit some person or persons in the corporation, but a corporation is made up of shareholders, management and the working force.
If a company makes profits, someone must benefit. If the workers receive more income, they pay more income tax. If management receives more, they also must pay further income tax so that the federal and provincial treasuries benefit. Before dividends are paid, a corporation tax of 40 to 50 per cent must also be paid and if citizens receive dividends, they in turn must pay income tax. The corporations cannot have depreciation allowances that are not also available to unincorporated individuals in business or to the great cooperatives which pay no corporation tax and are able to pass along dividends to their shareholders or patrons without a corporation tax.
Those who feel that corporations and other firms of private enterprise are bad for the country must agree that things should be better because over 50 per cent of our GNP is now being spent by the three levels of government. There are vast areas of the so-called private sector filled with Crown corporations such as CNR, Air Canada and public utilities such as the provincially owned telephone systems. Those utilities which are privately owned have rigid rate structures set by the governments concerned. Even the agriculture industry, with many individual farmers, has a myriad of boards, mostly government, con-
The Address-Mr. Cullen
trolling the sale of their products and setting the price the producer wiil receive.
All investment counsellors will tell you that the largest single factor in the investment market is the employees' pension funds, mutual funds and insurance funds, all designed to gather in the savings of the small person and to have them invested in the market by managements. When we talk about corporate rip-offs and excessive corporate profits, we are also talking about the earning in these employees' pension funds, mutual funds and insurance funds and saying they are too high. In the few minutes that were available to me, I hurriedly put forward a few ideas on what I feel is the role of a member in this speech from the throne debate and the important part of that speech which is being discussed today.

Mr. Speaker, I am happy to have the opportunity to participate in the throne speech debate. My first words must be words of congratulation to the mover and the seconder of the Address in Reply to the Speech from the Throne. Several years ago I had that distinction myself. At that time the Right Hon. Rolland Michener was Governor General of this country. I commented at that time on what a distinguished career he had and what a force he had been in that particular role. I, along with all of my colleagues, am satisfied that the right choice has been made for his successor. I look forward to the role that the new Governor General will play in that particular office. As one who had some dealing with him when he was with the office of the Secretary of State, I remember being very impressed with the careful manner with which he dealt with each problem brought before him, and the courtesy he extended to people who were dealing with him. I am sure he will bring that kind of dedication and courtesy to his office.
The Speech from the Throne makes reference to the petrochemical industry. As one who represents an area which has sometimes been called the chemical valley of Canada, it was heartening indeed to see that specific reference in the throne speech. Shortly after 1968, when I became a member of parliament, I made it my business to meet with officials who, in some circles, have become known as bad people, multinational corporation executives and members of boards of directors, to find out about the petrochemical industry, what problems it was facing and what was being done to help it because when the petrochemical industry in Canada is strong, there are a lot of people who have reason to be thankful, not only the shareholders and management, but the people who work for the corporations.
We had a sad experience in Sarnia. It was necessary to lay off something like 100 employees of Polymer, now Polysar, people who felt they were in a secure position. They were not worried about being laid off, but they soon learned the effects of being laid off. Some people had 18 to 20 years experience with that particular corporation. If anything highlighted the problems being faced by the petrochemical industry, that certainly was the spotlight that pointed me to the target area about which we should be doing something.
At that time it was very heartening to know that the Hon. Jean-Luc Pepin was Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce. After speaking to him, I found that the compa-

March 11, 1974
The Address-Mr. Cullen
nies and the government had decided to stop warring with one another and do what could be done to help the petrochemical industry. A joint government-chemical industry committee was established, not to deal with recriminations but to determine the problems being faced by the petrochemical industry and what it was within the power of the Canadian governments to do about it.
At that time there was some concern that it was the size of the market that was having a disastrous effect on the size of the industry. It was not possible to build one world-scale plant, yet you might have several companies which felt that in order to get feed stock prices down to a particular level it was necessary to build plants on a world-scale level. Therefore, they looked at this.
Arising out of the report handed down by the joint government-chemical industry committee came the opportunity for not one, but two world-scale plants. These will have the beneficial effect of giving to the petrochemical industry feed stocks at competitive prices. That is all the petrochemical industry was asking. They wanted an opportunity to compete on an equal base or slightly less advantageous than the Americans. They said they could do it because they had the men, women, machinery, technology and skills. All they needed was world-scale plant. Of course, if it was possible to secure a larger market, that was to be not only the responsibility of the companies but of the Canadian government.
The beauty of the petrochemical industry is that, despite what has been said and reported for some years, the petrochemical industry is developing, and not only in the Sarnia-Lambton area. I suggest with respect, hoping not to be too parochial, that the Sarnia petrochemical complex constitutes the real heartbeat of the industry and that when this particular section is strong the whole petrochemical industry is strong. I was heartened to note the Dow-Dome people had made an application to the National Energy Board and this will lead, if the application is allowed, to the construction of a world-scale plant in Alberta producing feedstock in the order of one billion pounds per annum. This is the kind of operation that is very helpful to Alberta. It will not only have a world-scale sized plant but, as a result of that one plant being there, derivative plants are likely to be constructed. It seems to me, Mr. Speaker, if the operation is strong in Alberta it will work to the benefit of the petrochemical industry in Ontario and in Quebec.
It may not be the national dream of a national railway but I would suggest, with respect, that a strong petrochemical industry is good for all of Canada. Four companies are now, I believe, about to embark on an application for the construction of a world-scale plant called the SOAP plant for purposes of brevity. The SOAP plant at the present time I assume, is making an application to the National Energy Board. This will have the effect of building or creating a world-scale plant for the production of ethylene. I am somewhat concerned about what impact it might have on Esso chemical who are at the present time meeting, as far as they are able, the needs of the petrochemical industry. But it seems to me, given todays booming economy, that this will not work to the detriment of Esso chemical but that Esso will, in fact, be

able to pick up at a considerable amount of market, since most, if not all, of the products to be available from the SOAP operation, will not meet the market at the time that plant comes into production.
I have to comment at this point about the 40 per cent tax rate, the reduction which was given to the manufacturing association. This was an area that caused some concern to me, because a promise was made by the government in May, 1972. and after the results of the election in October, 1972 were known the Minister of Finance (Mr. Turner) could I think quite justifiably have said "No, we can't go ahead with this; the people have indicated that they do not support it". But this Liberal government had made a commitment to business, and I was very proud of the fact that the Minister of Finance saw fit to honour that obligation; he did not wait for several months of discussion, but indicated almost immediately thereafter that this particular tax rate would become law. I do not know what the end result will be; we shall have to wait until the end of March. But it seems to me from anything that I have been able to read in the business sections of various newspapers, and in trade journals, and from what I heard the minister himself say earlier today, that 110,000 more jobs have been created in this particular industry, which seems to speak for itself as to the correctness of the action taken by this government.
I suspect, if I may look into the future, the report will indicate that there has in fact been a large capital expenditure by the manufacturing industry as a direct result of this 40 per cent figure. I am pleased to see the Minister of Finance had the guts, the good sense and the honesty, to go ahead with this particular commitment made prior to the October election. I do not often agree with the hon. member for Dauphin (Mr. Ritchie), but I have to agree with him that there seems to be a ham-handed effort in progress on the part of the New Democratic Party to give Canadian business a black eye. This is of some concern to me, Mr. Speaker, because, as the hon. member for Dauphin has said, when you give corporations which are creating jobs a black eye, you are giving it also to the people who invest in that company; you are making them uneasy, suggesting to them that perhaps they are investing their money in the wrong direction.
They are looking for a fair return on their investments. They are not looking for excessive profits. Selective use of statistics bothers me because it only leads to part of the truth being told. The figures are probably correct but I have learned to look with some suspicion on statistics ever since they were described to me as being like a bikini bathing suit-what they reveal is interesting but what they conceal is vital. I think we owe it to Canadians to see to it that multinational corporations do not become too strong. I think we are under an obligation to impose controls where controls are necessary, using the fiscal and monetary weapons at our disposal, to see to it that they act as good Canadian corporate citizens. I believe this is our responsibility because they are so strong. But by the same token I think there is a glorious opportunity to take advantage of the presence of these multinational corporations, bearing in mind that they do many splendid things for this country.
March 11, 1974

Unhappily, the right wingers in this House have been content to say very little on the subject. I think of myself as a left wing Liberal, certainly left of centre, and 1 am surprised that hon. members who hold themselves out to be Conservatives and right wing in their views have not yet seen fit to refute some of the statements made by the New Democrats. It is time we devoted a day to a good debate on this subject in order to hear not only their viewpoint but other points of view. Let us get out all the statistics and find out what really is happening. If there are abuses, they can be controlled. But to suggest the picture is all black is, surely, going too far. The NDP remind me of certain people who profess to be experts without any practical experience. None of them, to my knowledge, have ever run a business. They remind me of child psychologists who have never had children of their own but who can tell us how children should be raised.
Although I represent primarily an urban constituency I wish to speak for a few moments about the situation in which Canadian cattlemen find themselves at the present time.
Have you ever raised any cattle?
Oh, oh!
The hon. member asks me whether I have raised any cattle. I want to say that I have spread a little bull in my time.
Hear, hear!

Mr. Speaker, I had the opportunity to serve as chairman on the committee on food prices, so it may seem ironic I should be suggesting the imposition of some form of control over cattle imports. If low prices give rise to a situation in which a large proportion of Canadian cattle production is destroyed, the consumer is bound to suffer in the long run. We are obliged to make sure that this does not happen. Even if we pay a little more by way of higher prices it will be money well spent, and will ultimately reflect to the benefit of consumers.
The Speech from the Throne tells us that supplies must be increased. Undoubtedly this is the way to cope with rising prices. We all saw the disastrous effect of imposing controls at a time when supplies were short-they act in the long run to the detriment of the consumer. I disagree with the position taken by NDP speakers that the Food Prices Review Board should be given the authority to roll back prices. Any action in that regard should be taken by the government itself, and the government should be directly responsible in the House. In my view it would be wrong for a government to shelter behind the Food Prices Review Board. Any obligation to roll back prices rests with the government not with an appointed tribunal. I do not see the Food Prices Review Board in such a role.
While I am on this subject, I should like to commend the Food Prices Review Board. Many who are critical of this board never bother to read its reports. 1 refer particularly to a recent report on the effect of controls in Britain and the United States. I have the opinion that the board is served by an excellent research staff. Critics of the board
The Address-Mr. Carter
should at least take time to read its reports before they sound off.
In the field of veterans' affairs, I am concerned about three issues. The first is, whether or not the date for the receipt of applications under certain veterans' legislation ought to be extended. I hope this will be very carefully studied. Second, I think the transfer of hospitals is a good idea and I support it. However, I am apprehensive that eventually our veterans will reach the age where young doctors will not be entering veterans hospitals but will be dealing with senior citizens, therefore the veterans will not be getting the specialized treatment that they should have. By the same token, I am concerned that we should not forget that they are veterans hospitals.
I recommend to the minister that serious consideration be given to appointing an ombudsman to supervise all hospitals, or that each hospital have an ombudsman. I can say from my own experience with veterans that some of the veterans now being treated in veterans hospitals are afraid to raise a ruckus because they feel they might be sent home early or that they would only cause trouble for themselves. I do not think this sort of situation should be allowed to exist, and this is why I suggest an ombudsman.
The last matter I want to raise 1 have raised over and over again. Statistics on the backlog of pension cases being cleaned up are impressive, but I think that even more haste is required in this area.
I should like to go on, Mr. Speaker, but I see my time is up.

speakeroldname: Mr. Walter C. Carter (St. John's West):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, at the outset, may I welcome to the gallery this afternoon a group of young Newfoundland students under the Reverend Brother Brennan who are visiting their capital from Corner Brook and several other communities around that area.
In rising to take part in this debate I should like, first of all, to associate myself with the other members of the House who have paid tribute to the new Governor General and Mrs. Leger. On behalf of my constituents and my province I wish them good health, success and happiness during their term of office. I am sure I am expressing the feelings of my constituents and my province when I say how much we look forward to a visit by His Excellency and Mrs. Leger in what we hope will be the not too distant future. I join with my colleagues in extending my sincere congratulations to the mover and seconder of the address in reply. Considering how little these two hon. members had to work with, I think they did a very good job and excelled themselves in their speeches.
I should also like to congratulate my leader, the Leader of the Official Opposition (Mr. Stanfield), on the brilliant speech he made during this debate. I am sure that he was echoing the feelings and beliefs of the vast majority of Canadians who have been confronted with, and will continue to be confronted with, unemployment, high living costs and inflation generally.
The Speech from the Throne, not unlike the one delivered last year, held no real surprises. There is nothing in the speech to instil any real confidence in our people.
382

March 11, 1974
The Address-Mr. Carter
Noticeably absent from the speech is any meaningful indication of resource policy, trade and income policy, monetary policy and, what is more important, any policy of worth to fight inflation. We must recognize the fact that unless the problems of inflation are eliminated no other domestic problems in this country will be solved. Therefore, it stands to reason that it should be the first priority of this government to tackle inflation.
What do we have before us, Mr. Speaker? We have a speech that indicates quite clearly that this government are content to go their merry way in the belief that we are merely the victims of world wide inflation. They are content to bury their heads in the sand and let things ride on the basis that all of our problems are the direct result of inflationary pressures from outside this country, that the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau), this government, and indeed the people of Canada, are innocent bystanders. The people of Canada, particularly those in the middle and low income brackets, are not buying any longer the excuses and indifference of this government. If the Prime Minister and his colleagues have been listening to responses from the people of Canada, it will become abundantly clear to them that it is time they got down from their academic ivory towers and started to mix with the bare facts of reality.
The first thing that this government must do is to be honest with itself and with the people and recognize the fact that inflation in Canada is not the total responsibility of outside forces, but that there exist in this country problems that are adding to inflation. This government must change its defeatist attitude; there is no use trying to change this situation when the people responsible are not convinced themselves that change can come about. The government must be willing to admit to themselves, and to the people, that their handling of the situation has been wrong. It is no tragedy to admit failure. To err is human. But to continue in the full knowledge that you are wrong, and without regard for the future welfare of millions of our people, is a tragedy and is inhuman.
It will be essential for this government and for the people of this country to work together in order to get out of the mess in which we now find ourselves. A short-term freeze on certain elements of the Canadian economy is essential if we are serious about fighting inflation. This must be followed by an economic, income and monetary policy. One without the other will not work, but together they will work. If this government is serious about the future welfare of Canadians, then it is time it swallowed its pride and listened to the people. It is time it implemented the policy for fighting inflation put forth by the leader of our party.
I listened with a great deal of interest for some mention in the throne speech of the government's objectives in regard to the development of the food producing segments of our economy. Being a Newfoundlander I was, of course, particularly interested in the government's objectives as they relate to the fisheries. May I quote this extract from the Speech from the Throne:
The government's objectives will guide a re-assessment of existing programs in the areas of agriculture and fisheries.
This, sir, is the first mention of fisheries in the speech. Other references to fisheries relate to the government's

intention to improve harbour facilities for fishing fleets and the promise of guaranteed loans and other forms of assistance to both farmers and fishermen to assist them in purchasing or modernizing their equipment. The throne speech also promised incentives to increase Canada's catch of unexploited stocks of fish. I hope that the government's reassessment of the agriculture industry has been more productive and meaningful than their reassessment of the fishing industry. Otherwise, I am afraid we will have more than empty stockings next Christmas; we will have empty bread baskets and probably empty stomachs as well.
What I am about to say now I have said before, because last year the same situation prevailed. I refer to the government's expenditures on badly needed small craft harbour facilities in the Atlantic area. Let us for a moment translate into actual fact the government's promise to improve harbour facilities for our fishing fleets. For the benefit of hon. members who are not familiar with the problem, I should point out that harbour and wharf facilities are to our fishermen what grain elevators, storage facilities and boxcars are to our western farmers. Without these facilities our wheat farmers cannot produce and successfully market their crops. By the same token, without adequate harbour and fish landing facilities our fishermen cannot produce or attain their full potential in the fishing industry.
The entire federal budget this year for the provision and improvement of small craft harbour facilities is less than that being spent by the government in the city of Ottawa on the acquisition of properties on Sparks Street. Indeed, in Newfoundland, where there is such a desperate need for these facilities, the federal government proposes to spend approximately $4.2 million during the coming fiscal year. That is approximately the same amount being spent by this government on the provision of an underground parking facility in the city of Hull.
On March 6 last, I received a letter from the Minister of Fisheries and the Environment (Mr. Davis) to which he attached a list of the works to be undertaken by his department during the 1974-75 fiscal year, together with a list of other projects that have been considered essential but, according to him, will of necessity be deferred due to budget constraints. The cost of the projects selected for the 1974-75 program for my constituency amount to $445,000. The cost of the projects that have been deferred, notwithstanding their urgency, amounts to $1.5 million. How naive does the Minister of Fisheries think we are? Is it any wonder that our people have lost faith in this government and are fed up to the teeth with what is taking place in this country today? Is it any wonder that there is a growing resentment among a large segment of our people in respect of the present government and its attitude toward the have-not regions of this country?
Fishing facilities are vitally important to Newfoundland and, indeed, to other fishing areas in this country. Without them fishermen are unable to fish productively and make a living for themselves from this industry. Does the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) expect us to accept, without question, the extravagant spending on the part of his government in certain areas when primary producers including fishermen are told to eat cake? Does he expect us to accept

without a murmur the huge amounts of money provided for in this year's estimates for the acquisition of properties in and around the capital for the provision of bigger and better public buildings, and for bilingualism which this year is costing the Canadian taxpayer in excess of $200 million while the real problems of this country are being swept under the carpet?
Oh, come on.

The fishermen of my constituency are being denied their fundamental right of being able to earn a living from the fisheries, while at the same time we see in the estimates typical examples of this government's misguided sense of priorities. It is no wonder that a lot of Canadians are getting fed up with this government's preoccupation with matters that are receiving priority such as those I have mentioned. As I have said, this year alone we will spend in excess of $200 million on bilingualism in Canada. This represents about 9 per cent of the government's budget. I am not suggesting for a moment that there is no need for a policy on bilingualism in Canada. I think we all recognize that need and members of this party have gone along with the proposition, but I do believe there are times when other things should take priority, and this also applies to certain areas of the province of Quebec. Certainly, in the Atlantic area there are problems which should not be deferred in favour of other programs the government has seen fit to initiate and finance.
Speak for yourself.

It must be obvious to the Prime Minister and to his government that not enough attention is being paid to the needs, wishes and desires of the people, and I include the fishermen of eastern Canada who are in many cases being denied their basic rights as citizens of this country.
Our concern in eastern Canada, certainly in my province, is not in respect of cultural sovereignty. That is something we probably will start worrying about in 50 years' time. We are concerned about the right to be treated equally as Canadians, and the right to earn a decent living. I am sure that statement will shatter the delicate ears of some of my colleagues opposite but, be that as it may, I can assure you I am not alone in that view.
That's a lot of bull and you know it.

speakerposition: Deputy House Leader of the Official Opposition; Progressive Conservative Party Deputy House Leader
speechtext: You wouldn't know a bull from a flounder.
Mr. Speaker, the hon. member must be quite familiar with bull, so I will not deny him his right to say that.
Don't pretend to be the only one speaking for Atlantic Canada.

You will have your chance, and then perhaps you will stand up and be heard. These people have had enough of this government's costly policies. Of course, we know what is happening. The Prime Minister is not fooling us. We know it is the philosophy of the Prime Minister and the Liberal party to divide and conquer, to
The Address-Mr. Nelson
keep political power at any price, and that is what they are setting out to do. They are pitting one segment of our society against another. The Prime Minister is not content with that, he is now working on a program to pit the east against the west and region against region.
And fishermen against farmers.

Yes, and fishermen against farmers as my hon. colleague suggests. The Prime Minister is doing all this under the name and guise of national unity. Of course, his real reason is to retain the political power he has, and he is not too concerned about what the outcome will be so far as this country is concerned.
Let me tell the Prime Minister through you, Mr. Speaker, that he is playing a dangerous game. He is playing with fire. The majority of Canadians can see through this sinister plot and are not having any part of it. Indeed, the obvious philosophy that has been adopted by the Prime Minister and the Liberal government will have the opposite effect in this country in that it will be responsible for creating prejudices and bigotry. There is a lot of rumbling in this country and particularly in my province, as a result of this government's obvious intention and determination to reduce certain areas, including certain parts of the Atlantic region, to that of colonial status.
It is really paradoxical when one realizes that the government is spending hundreds of millions of dollars, allegedly to bring the people of Canada together, when on the other hand it is doing its best to alienate the people of other provinces, including Newfoundland, making them feel a non-part of the federal system. I refer, of course, to the policy of this government to reduce its presence in Newfoundland to that of a branch office with headquarters in one or other of the Atlantic provinces.

speakerposition: Assistant Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: Order, please. I regret to interrupt the hon. member, but his time has expired.

Mr. Speaker, if I begin my brief remarks with comments on the speeches of the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Stanfield) and the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau), I do so in the spirit of reflecting on their party policies and not on them as individuals.
I was not disappointed with the speech of the Leader of the Opposition because, as the saying goes, blessed is he who expects nothing for he shall not be disappointed. Perhaps the best part of his speech was the metaphor he used in describing members in the government benches as an orchestra, with various ministers playing designated instruments albeit discordantly, while he himself, like little Johnnie one note, sang the monotonous and discredited theme of the Tory party, wage and price controls. This term has been variously disguised as a prices and incomes policy, a freeze followed by unstated measures, or a freeze followed by specific measures which are never specific. Whatever term one falls for, this still means locking in the inequities that already exist and, as for the measures that follow the freeze, it is unlikely that the leopard will change his spots.
27398-25*

March 11, 1974
The Address-Mr. Nelson
There was a lot of meat in the speech of the Prime Minister who said:
Our problem is the equitable distribution of our most abundant wealth.
That is a beautiful statement. He went on to state:
I find it appropriate at this time to destroy the myth that the cost of labour has been a dominant factor in contributing to the present inflationary round in Canada.
That is a wonderful statement. Then, he fired his big gun and said:
We will not hesitate to go after the so-called big guys if action is necessary to protect the Canadian consumer.
These statements may come back to haunt the government in the months or weeks or days to come. Well, Mr. Speaker, let me emphasize now, as our leader already has and our members have over the months and during this debate, that action is necessary to protect the Canadian consumer. In 1973, as we all know, the consumer price index went up by 9.1 per cent, hitting the average family in the two most vital spots, food and housing, which together account for 56 per cent of average family income. The government admits that labour is not to blame, and statistics show that wage and salary increases in the last half of 1973 actually decreased by nearly one per cent while corporation profits, on the other hand, in 1973 were over-all 40 to 50 per cent higher than in 1972, which was a good year too.
I will not list the profit figures of the huge corporations because they are already a matter of public record. Despite the comments of the hon. member for Sarnia-Lambton (Mr. Cullen), we are not anti-business; we are anti-business abuse. Most multi-nationals could be included in that category. I remember our leader, during a speech in this House, complimenting a large Canadian corporation for its corporate business practice. The government said it would not hesitate to take action. In 1963, the three largest sugar importers were convicted of price fixing. Now, they are at it once more and are being prosecuted again. But in the intervening time, between 1963 and today, it is estimated that the price fixing activities of these three firms have cost the Canadian consumer $125 million. Now, there is hesitation for you-eight years of it. Now, the steel companies and the cement companies are under suspicion. Is it any wonder that we look askance at statements that promise action when necessary?
The public is beginning to catch on, but they know now what to expect of the oil companies. A recent Gallup poll conducted by the Canadian Institute of Public Opinion shows that over half of the Canadian public has lost confidence that the multinational oil companies will act in the interests of Canada. Anyone who has visited the United States lately will hear the same distrust widely expressed. Even there, the public is calling for investigations and for public control. Now, the wolves are starting to gather around the Athabasca tar sands. What will the government do to protect the interests of Canadians? Will they use the proposed national petroleum company to serve the interests of Canadians or will this be another sell-out of our national resources?
As the hon. member for Nanaimo-Cowichan-The Islands (Mr. Douglas) has pointed out, unless this government

gets into the oil business in co-operation with the provincial governments to place this huge resource under public control, the confidence that the oil companies have lost will extend to the government, as it probably has already. In light of the fantastic profits quoted by so many members on this side of the House, excluding the Tories who have their sights trained on smaller game, how can the government in the name of all that is reasonable deny the need for greater controls over the activities and profits of the large corporations.
The Tories complain about the high cost of welfare programs and of UIC, but do you ever hear them quote the $4.7 billion in deferred taxes to large corporations? They speak with feeling about the need for housing and of the plight of those who do not have decent shelter, but they seldom make specific mention of the 516 per cent increase in profits in 1973 of one of our largest real estate and development institutions and others like it. Yes, the Tories have their sights trained on smaller game. That champion of the working man, the hon. member for Hamilton West (Mr. Alexander) zeroed in only last Thursday on the extent to which people are 'cheating' or 'ripping-off' the Unemployment Insurance Commission. No one would condone cheating on UIC or any other program, but according to my information, in 1972 only 908 persons were prosecuted by UIC for having cheated on their claims. That is .05 per cent of all claims. As for the rip-off, I was interested to hear from no less an authority than the hon. member for Verdun (Mr. Mackasey), whose humanitarian approach to the workers seems incongruous in the context of the present minister's attitude that:
The people who went on unemployment insurance in 1972 with eight weeks work represented 2.5 per cent of all claims in Canada. That is what all the excitement is about-2.5 per cent, 11 weeks or less, 35,000 people.
Let the Tories fire their salvos, not at the working people but at the real rip-off artist whose embarrassingly high profits are published every day-the multinational corporations who manipulate the pricing and distribution of goods to their own advantage and the wealthy people in this country who, according to the Dominion Bureau of Statistics, under-report their investment income by as much as 50 per cent.
I want to mention pensions only briefly because the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) has already spoken and when he speaks he leaves nothing left for the rest of the seagulls. Since his speech, however, the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Lalonde) has made it clear that the government does not intend to lower the pensionable age. This news will come as a great shock and disappointment to thousands of weary Canadians who have worked hard all their lives and who desperately want to lay down their tools before age 65. The Canadian people want adequate pensions at age 60, and until a step is made in this direction, the remarks that the minister made this afternoon will have a hollow ring.
I have in the past 14 months worked closely with the claims officer in my own branch of the Canadian Legion. I have always found the Minister of Veterans Affairs (Mr. MacDonald) to be co-operative and I believe he is doing his best. I note that the processing of claims has been speeded up and the backlog reduced last year from 9,000 to 7,300. From the minister's point of view, and taking into
March 11, 1974

consideration the difficulties of processing which he evidently faces, this is no doubt a significant achievement. From the point of view of the needy applicant who is far down the list, however, settlement seems remote and time short. I thank the minister for past courtesies and urge him to bend even greater effort toward speeding up the processing of these claims.
One of the greatest achievements of past Liberal governments was the administration of the veteran's education rehabilitation program which concluded in the mid-fifties. I know this from personal experience. It would now be a most appropriate gesture on this 25th biennial convention year of the Royal Canadian Legion to extend the deadline for the Veterans Land Act, and I would hope that the government will consider doing so.
Now, Mr. Speaker, time is streaking by and because of the agreement to limit speeches at this stage I will make only brief reference to the problems of urban development in the lower mainland region of British Columbia. The Minister of State for Urban Affairs (Mr. Basford) has spoken of specific projects related to port development, and I am aware of the developments taking place to improve port facilities. I want to mention, however, a matter of particular concern to me and to many community groups in my riding, namely the future development of the Burrard Inlet east of the Second Narrows bridge. On both sides of the inlet there is an ever present danger that too much industrial and commercial development will result in congestion and environmental damage. I believe the communities involved should have greater representation on the local National Harbours Commission.
For my part, as the federal member representing both sides of the inlet in this sensitive area, I recognize the right of local councils to make decisions regarding the planning and development of the communities which they represent. For that reason, I have not raised my voice against the installation of yet another refinery on the Burnaby side or the projected development of a large commercial enterprise on the north side of the inlet. Yet, it is my feeling that this vital growth area stands at the crossroads at this point in time. I pray with all my heart that the federal government, the provincial government, the greater Vancouver regional district and, most important of all, the municipal governments will catch the vision of the future and, putting partisan politics aside, work together, in the words of the Minister of State for Urban Affairs (Mr. Basford) "to develop in a co-operative way good techniques of managing urban growth to avoid congestion and pollution". The four levels of government that I have mentioned can, with frequent consultation with community groups, so manage developments that the people of this area, which extends far out into the Fraser Valley, will be assured of the ultimate goal: the development of a truly livable region.
If I may conclude on a parochial note, may I finally beg the indulgence of the House to pay tribute to the fine work of the co-ordinators of the provincial debating finals which took place last week in Burnaby-Seymour. Winners from all provinces will compete in a national debating final in May here in Ottawa. This is an excellent national program for training future citizens and politicians, and
The Address-Mr. Hopkins
an excellent example of community involvement. I am proud also that Burnaby-Seymour has provided so many world skating champions through the fine work of the North Shore Winter Club.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of National Defence
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, first of all, along with the other members of the House, I should like to extend my congratulations and those of my constituents to Their Excellencies, the Governor General and his good lady, on taking office and wish them well. Secondly, I should like to congratulate the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau), the cabinet and the many members of the government caucus for their contribution to the throne speech debate and to a dynamic and useful program for the second session of the twenty-ninth parliament. There is one thing to which I do not pay much heed, and that is the criticism of rubber stamping that this party receives, but I can say on behalf of my own colleagues that every member is a part of the party in general.
Hear, hear!

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of National Defence
speechtext:
This session has been taken up, to a large degree, in discussions on petroleum and energy in Canada. But there is one thing that should be made very clear and kept foremost in everyone's mind and that is that over the years since the 1940's federal governments in Canada have been spending millions of dollars on nuclear energy research in this country. Today, we are foremost among the nations of the world in the development of nuclear power and its domestic uses.
One of the things that has not received nearly enough emphasis throughout 1973, and throughout the debate on the energy crisis in Canada, is the happy fact that Atomic Energy of Canada at Chalk River and Deep River, which I am glad to have in my constituency, is the mother of the most efficient and successful power source in the world today. Indeed, it is the mother of the entire Ontario Hydro plant in Pickering. Ontario Hydro had the courage to go ahead and make the decision to try it, but it was the expertise of Atomic Energy of Canada that has made that plant possible and will make other plants possible. In our constituency in particular, and in the country at large, we should be taking our hats off to the science community at Atomic Energy in Chalk River and Deep River, as well as the National Research Council for leading the way to a new and bountiful source of energy for the world.
Sometimes we become so involved with our own problems that we forget to tell people about our successes. We had a very famous Canadian in the past, who went down fighting in the election of 1957, in the person of the Right Hon. C. D. Howe. I should like to remind members of this House today of something that has probably long since been forgotten, but it was the Right Hon. C. D. Howe who was the initiator of Atomic Energy of Canada Limited. It is because of his initiative, in spite of the criticism that he received in this House and in spite of the fact that sometimes he arrived at decisions in a hurry but they were usually the right decisions, that one of the most expensive research institutions that we have in Canada was started, one which produced much good for mankind, not only in Canada but in the world at large. This nation owes him

March 11, 1974
The Address-Mr. Hopkins
thanks for taking leadership and for his courage back in the 1940's.
Hear, hear!

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of National Defence
speechtext: The Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. Macdonald) has been named "man of the year" by the business section of the Toronto Globe and Mail. He has carried himself well through a very difficult period and in the debates in the House of Commons. I do not care who laughs or what comments are made about him. He has taken a stand in this House and he has done his work well. He deserves the credit of the Canadian community.
Hear, hear!

speakerposition: Deputy House Leader of the Official Opposition; Progressive Conservative Party Deputy House Leader
speechtext: Especially the big companies.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of National Defence
speechtext:
Recently, I have had the honour to visit our Canadian armed forces in Europe where I had several briefings and visited our servicemen in the field. I have also had the privilege of visiting the U.N. forces in Cyprus. We now have a large contingent in Egypt. I do not think people really appreciate how difficult U.N work is for Canadian servicemen. It requires a lot of patience and great dedication. Our servicemen who serve in these positions around the world in the NATO forces and in our Canadian forces in Europe are to be commended to the nth degree for the image of this nation that they are giving around the world.
While in Cyprus I also had the opportunity to speak to some of the people on both sides of the conflict there. It still looks like a very difficult issue to settle. But there is one thing that must be said for the senior officers as well as the rank and file in the armed forces, and that is that regardless of the tasks they are given to do, they take these tasks seriously. In spite of the problems with which they are faced, they go ahead and do the job.
I would be remiss if I did not say a few words about the Department of Regional Economic Expansion and the work it has done in parts of eastern Ontario. In the upper part of the Ottawa valley, a large section of which I have the privilege of representing, as well as in other areas that I do not represent directly, such as the towns of Renfrew, Arnprior, Eganville and so on, if it was not for DREE and its input into that region we would not be getting ahead nearly as well as we are today. In spite of all the criticism this department has received from various areas across Canada, it is welcome in our section of eastern Ontario any day. I will stand up in the House and support the minister any day.
In the new agreements that will be forthcoming on DREE, some of which have already been made, I hope there will be a considerable input and that my area of eastern Ontario will continue to benefit.
Mr. Speaker, I would be very remiss if I did not congratulate the mayors, the reeves, the industrial commissioners and the people who have really tried to make this system work. We all know that it is one thing for government to bring in policies, but it is another thing for the people in the local areas to pick up the ball and carry it

down the field, making use of those policies. I hope we continue to have strong and dedicated people in municipal governments in this part of Canada, and indeed across the country. Sometimes we do not give municipal politicians the credit they deserve.
Mr. Speaker, I wanted to make a further point about the town of Deep River. Because of the existence of large plants of Atomic Energy of Canada Limited at Chalk River and Deep River, which employ 2,450 people, it is sometimes thought by both senior levels of government that since the town of Deep River receives a grant in lieu of taxes from that Crown corporation the town does not qualify for the award of other grants. This is unfair to the town. It has been in existence since the 1940's and now requires a lot of money for maintenance as well as growth. I do not feel that the existence of that grant in lieu of taxes from AECL should be used as an argument to refuse the town of Deep River the same grants it should normally receive, just as any other community of its size across Canada.
There have been many discussions inside and outside this House in regard to the LIP program and the minister has come under fire about some projects. We have to realize that human beings are not perfect, not 100 per centers. In spite of the criticism that has been levied at the odd LIP program, in my estimation it has been one of the most successful programs for providing services and worthwhile work in small communities that would otherwise be absolutely forgotten.
There are many small communities scattered throughout my constituency, which is the largest of 77 in southern Ontario. I would not be ashamed to take anybody to any part of my riding to show them the work undertaken through the Local Initiatives Program to service the small communities. I hope the criticism, which has been overemphasized, of particular projects, that have failed will not be used as a sledgehammer to kill a program as a result of which much good work has been accomplished.
Mr. Speaker, a part of the Speech from the Throne dealt with freight rates and freight policies across Canada. These are probably equally important to the DREE program. Many industries have been assisted in settling in various parts of Canada, but perhaps they should be encouraged into slow growth areas with a freight rate policy that would assist in their success. This is the way to put permanency into the usefulness of the DREE program, and I do not think we can talk about the one without talking about the other. We have also a key role to play in providing roads for transportation, and I hope that greater emphasis will be placed on this in eastern Ontario in the future as an enticement to economic development.
Earlier, Mr. Speaker, I mentioned that our forces in Europe, Cyprus and Egypt are dedicated but their job is a very trying one which demands a great deal of patience. When talking to the men in the field I realized that the one thing they missed was sports news, hockey results and so on from Canada; things which are a way of Canadian life. Upon my return I wrote to a major oil company in Canada to ask if it would sponsor tapes and video taped programs for the armed forces in Europe, Cyprus and Egypt. I sincerely hope that this will work, and if it does I
March 11, 1974

will be approaching the appropriate ministries to assist in bringing these facilities to the armed forces overseas.
There are many things that our armed forces do of which people are not aware. For example, in the preservation of ecology, our maritime aircraft and naval vessels monitor pollution on our coasts and report major offenders to the appropriate government department for action. I had a very interesting experience approximately two weeks ago in visiting Maritime Command.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: Order, please. I regret that I must interrupt the hon. member but the time allotted to him has expired.

Mr. Speaker, I should like to take this opportunity to offer my congratulations and good wishes to His Excellency the Governor General. I think that the installation of our new Governor General reminds the country of the importance of his office, and the Crown which he represents, an importance that over the years has been lost sight of by the government of this country, until very recently. We are aware of how the government began to take a new look at the monarchy and the representation of it after October 30, 1972. I think it is fair to say in a quarter of a century before that, that a series of Liberal governments had reduced the importance of the monarchy, it is vital for us to take this occasion to recall the importance of the Crown and the parliamentary system, to recognize the tactical value it has in the way our country is governed.
I think one of the lessons that we, as Canadians, can learn from Watergate is that in the parliamentary system we have a far superior form of government, and basic to that system is the function and role of the Crown.
I wish to congratulate both the mover and the seconder of the address in reply to the Speech from the Throne. The hon. member for Spadina (Mr. Stollery) and the hon. member for Sherbrooke (Mr. Pelletier) set forth their case with clarity, conviction and sincerity, although with somewhat misguided enthusiasm for the subject on which they had to speak. Both hon. member made fine speeches.
I wish, in passing, to refer to the address of the hon. member for Sherbrooke because it was in great contrast to some of the speeches I have heard by other hon. members from his province, speeches which have contained inflammatory language, which have shown a derogatory spirit on the language issue. That attitude should not be brought to this House and should not be evident in this country. What we need, as some of us recognize, is that issue to be taken outside the realm of controversy and party competition. I regret that some of the remarks made on the Speech from the Throne have done little but contribute to the ill-will and misunderstandings of the past.
Most serious of all is the way in which the Speech from the Throne has failed to give the people of Canada and members of this parliament the sense of direction which we need because of the critical situation which Canadians face. The speech has been described by many commentators as lacking rhetoric. It certainly lacks a program. The country can stand absence of eloquence; it cannot endure an absence of understanding. At this point in Canada's
The Address-Mr. Stackhouse
history we need leadership. The country does not need a government which give top priority to its own survival: it needs a government that will give it a sense of direction.
I recognize that it is scarcely possible to find this sense of direction under a government which cannot decide whether it should follow the Liberal direction or the socialist direction. The country cannot be given that direction if the government does not know its own direction. This is of vital concern to us all because of the crisis situation in which this country now finds itself.
When a general election is held in Canada, and held it must be despite the chameleon adaptiveness of the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau), the choice for Canadians primarily will not be between two parties but between two ways of life. One way of life is to be seen by the present alliance between Liberals and socialists. It is based upon the conviction that the government should be a kind of Big Brother, at the centre of life, and take over every aspect of life of the Canadian people. That way of life we see demonstrated in the way in which the role of government is expanding in Canada under the present administration which is taking on behemoth proportions.
It is now expected that the public service of Canada will expand to over 330,000 employees in the forthcoming fiscal year. If we add the members of the armed forces and others directly or indirectly on the federal payroll, we find that there will be working for the federal government directly or for the public service, including Crown corporations, in the neighbourhood of 500,000 persons, representing 5 per cent of the labour force of this country. The cost of that massive force mounts every year. The bill for the federal government is rising at a speed 50 per cent greater than the growth of the gross national product. The federal budget is such that there is now a levy on each person, adult and child, of $1,000 or more per year. The cost of living for Canadians last year increased by 9.5 per cent, but the cost of government will increase by more than 20 per cent.
I ask this question: what do Canadians have to show for this? Much of this increase in cost is based upon the faith claim made by supporters of the government that whatever problem the people face, the government knows best what the solution ought to be. Name a single need which Canadians have experienced and you will find there has been some attempt by the government to present a fully funded program to deal with it. We have agencies, boards, commissions, corporations and groups of all kinds drawing on the public purse. We have projects, coalitions, organizations and committees, all reaching out with open hands for federal grants.
We have poured billions of dollars into programs for removing regional disparities, eliminating slums, creating employment and improving the quality of life. Yet Canada still has deprived regions, substandard housing, jobless persons, mounting rates of crime, marriage breakdowns, drug addiction and alcohol abuse. It is clear that the spending of more and more public money by the federal government is not going to meet the needs of the Canadian people. We see that, for example, in the escalating costs of prisons. Last year the cost of operating our penitentiary service increased. The cost of keeping an inmate in prison has risen from $11,000 per year to $13,000 per year.

March 11, 1974
The Address-Mr. Stackhouse
When we debated this issue in the previous session of parliament, I hazarded the prediction that if the rate of increase in the cost of running our penitentiary service continued to the end of this decade, by the end of the 1970's we would be spending $20,000 per inmate per year. I was wrong: we will reach that figure by 1978 if we continue to escalate costs at the present rate. Yet we see no indication of the government being aware that these expenditures do not achieve what they purport to achieve. The government has inflated the cost of its penitentiary program in order to put greater emphasis on rehabilitation. That aim I am sure all parties support. Certainly I do. Yet in exchange for the great expenditure the government has put out we have had little that is effective under the heading of rehabilitation. Actually, despite all the expenditures on our prisons, we have a recidivism rate of 80 per cent, which means that 80 per cent of the inmates of our penitentiaries have been in a penal institution previously. We find that instead of being rehabilitated, progressing and developing as normal citizens, a great proportion of prison inmates return to the penitentiary.
I cite this example to show that in one area undiminished growth in government expenditures will not achieve the objective which the government claims as justification for the growth in expenditure. In the Speech from the Throne I find no hint that the government will conduct a major re-examination of penitentiary services and the penal system in our country. Editorials in the Toronto Globe and Mail and the Toronto Star in recent weeks have reflected analytically and critically on the increased cost of our prisons and on the failure of our prisons to deliver the rehabilitative goods.
Those newspapers have challenged the government to face this issue honestly and to see if there are not more effective ways in which the public purse can be protected and offenders against the law dealt with. In this matter we have another example of the way in which the government is spending, spending, spending without being able to demonstrate to the public that in exchange for the massive outlay in public funds it is able to deliver the goods which it has set out to deliver. I hope, therefore, this House of Commons will be far more critical of the attempts by the government to inflate the federal budget.
[DOT] (mo)
One of the facts of life in Canada today that the government has refused to recognize is the hard fact that a major element in the high cost of living is the high cost of governing, and that the government of Canada is itself a contributor to the inflationary crisis that is now affecting the people of Canada. The hon. member who preceded me spoke with some enthusiasm about the way in which all Liberal members of parliament contribute to the thinking of the Liberal government. One gets the impression that the caucus of the government party is one great, expanded cabinet meeting. If that is so, it would certainly be salutary and in the interest of the people of Canada if more and more Liberal members had an economizing influence upon their high-spending ministers.
One thing that has become clear to the people of Canada is that they are being required by the taxation process to put more money into their government and they are not getting back from the government the kind of service to

justify this outrageous expenditure. For example, I have here editorials from the Ottawa Citizen commenting upon the growth of the federal budget. The Ottawa Citizen states it is costing us more for the public service to do less. The Montreal Star refers to the way in which thousands of persons have been added to the federal civil service, while the service gets worse.
We have to realize that across this country it is becoming more and more clear that simply having a program initiated by the government at extraordinary expense will not meet the needs of the people. We must recognize that it is time we had a government that has some trust in the people of Canada and which recognizes that if the people of Canada could have more of their own hard-earned income remaining in their hands, they would be able to deal more effectively with their own problems.
We need to replace the Big Brother complex of this government, which believes that it primarily has the right and capacity for meeting the needs of the Canadian people, with one that recognizes the Canadian people have within their competence the wherewithal to meet their needs and to deal with their problems. What they require most is some freedom by which they can have more control over the income for which they have laboured. The Big Brother mentality of Liberal socialism that now governs Canada is robbing each taxpayer of that for which he has laboured.
If this parliament were really serving the needs of the people of Canada it would be seeking a program, enunciated in a throne speech, that would emphasize the way in which a government ought to trust the people of Canada. We have had too much Big Brother government: what we need is more faith in the people.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like to join other hon. members in congratulating the mover and seconder of the Address in reply to the Speech from the Throne, the hon. member for Spadina (Mr. Stollery), and the hon. member for Sherbrooke (Mr. Pelletier).
They showed that they are not only able parliamentarians but also that they can speak with conviction and are concerned with current problems, not only with those within their constituencies but also with those that concern us as Canadians and citizens of the world.
Mr. Speaker, as my time is limited, I shall spend less time than usual on discussing the Speech from the Throne, especially when dealing with my constituency and its problems. I shall restrict my comments to one problem, which I believe is a very important one at this time. Even if this is not a local problem, one which concerns only my constituency, in view of its importance at the national level and the effects that it could have on my constituents, I shall deal mostly with unemployment insurance, with the criticisms aimed at this system and with the famous reforms and investigations that some people in this country, particularly the members of the Progressive Conservative Party, would like to see undertaken.

Before doing that we must deal with one other issue that has been discussed in this debate and all over the country. That is the issue of inflation and rising costs in Canada. I
March 11, 1974

wish to put on the record-I will not use the word "stupid"-how illogical is the position of the Progressive Conservative Party with regard to inflation and rising costs.
There is no evidence at this time of cost-push inflation. The inflation is being caused by extreme shortages, not only in Canada but in the world. To suggest the simplistic solution of wage and price controls only because it is an appealing political slogan is very irresponsible. The Conservative Party says it has its roots in regions of this country including my own area in the maritimes. They want to freeze the salaries of the people in my constituency and in other parts of the maritimes. These people work for $2 an hour, and sometimes less. Even if they earn $2.50 an hour, how will their problems of inflation be solved by freezing their salaries for 90 days? That is not only ridiculous but irresponsible.
Hear, hear!

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources
speechtext:
Members from Newfoundland and Nova Scotia have been talking about the terrible rise in food prices. The price of fish in Newfoundland, New Brunswick and Nova Scotia has never been so high. For the first time in my short experience I can see fishermen getting a fair price for their catch. They are finally receiving a good income with which to support their families. However, the Conservatives would like not only to freeze the price of their product but their income.
I can cite figures to show that salaries of fish plant workers in Newfoundland and New Brunswick are about $3 an hour for the first time in the history of the maritimes. However, the Conservatives are saying to these people that they will solve their problems by freezing their income. Not only does it not make sense from an economic point of view, because it has failed in Britain, the United States and anywhere else where it has been tried, and not only is it stupid, but how can those people talk about social justice on the one hand and policies like that on the other?
Oh, oh!

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources
speechtext: The hon. member for Mississauga (Mr. Blenkarn) comes from the Toronto area where people earn $5 or $6 an hour. He does not understand what it is like to work in a fish plant for $2 an hour. I can appreciate his position. However, even if there were no members of his party from areas of the country where people work for low wages, I thought he would have enough heart not to suggest economic policies which mean that poor people have to bear the cost.
That is unfair.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources
speechtext: I wanted to speak about unemployment insurance because again we hear the same two standards expressed by the Conservatives-
The same old bunch over there.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources
speechtext:
Time and time again members on the opposition benches bring up errors in administration, dramatizing everything that occurs. The Liberals brought in this
The Address-Mr. Breau
program in 1971 at a time when they were in a majority position in the House. We did so because we believed it was good legislation, a step toward social justice; and we did so because the labour movement in Canada has failed to organize or to represent poor workers. It is well known that the labour movement has not succeeded in organizing strong labour movements among the poor.
When the Liberal government brought in the new act in 1971, a measure of social justice was brought to these people for the first time. By doing so we ensured that those workers, too, would enjoy a degree of independence of the kind possessed by workers in the riding of the hon. member for Mississauga who can bargain successfully for $5 or $6 an hour and compensation in the event of lay-offs. In my constituency, the large majority of workers do not have that power.
I should like to read part of an article by Mr. James Stewart which appeared in the Montreal Star. We have heard a great deal of nonsense about employers in New Brunswick and elsewhere being unable to get workers because of the effect of unemployment insurance benefits. That picture is completely false. I have lived in New Brunswick all my life and I know a great many poor people, people who draw unemployment benefits, and I have yet to meet a man who has refused a well paid and secure job. It is true that I have met people who have refused jobs that I would not give to a slave. It has been stated that because of unemployment insurance, employers cannot get workers in the fish processing or the forest industries. The article to which I referred states the following with reference to a study which was made of the forest industry in New Brunswick:
Out of approximately 550 persons identified as having left employment in the forest industry, only some 90 have been identified as drawing unemployment insurance benefits.
This means that some 460 people left for other reasons. Many industries have been asking people to work like slaves.
