When members constantly raise questions directing attention to weaknesses of administration, they should remember that when we brought in the new act we had to merge two acts together. When that is done, problems are bound to arise. Critics are playing upon the fears and, in some instances, upon the hate of those who are against this system of aiding the less fortunate in society. They are encouraging those who wish to destroy any program which gives defenceless workers a chance to become more independent. A lot of workers in my constituency have become more independent because of the UIC. I do not apologize for this. Neither do I apologize for those associated with the labour movement in other parts of the country who can bargain from strength and achieve security and a decent standard of living. Many people in my constituency no longer have to go out into the woods in December, January and February in six or seven feet of snow. They can draw benefits-
In other words, they don't have to work.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources
speechtext:
Would the hon. member who made that comment like a job in the woods, in seven feet of snow at forty bucks a week? Could he live on that? This is what has happened over the years. We have given people a
390

March 11, 1974
The Address-Mr. Wise
chance to become independent. In the past they were exploited. I am not saying there are no weaknesses in the act or in the work of the commission. There are bound to be some administrative weaknesses. But I draw it to your attention, Mr. Speaker, that last year a new concept was introduced into UIC administration-I forget the English term, but in French it is called "le concept d'administra-tion par modules ou les modules administratifs." The administration of the UIC offices was broken up in such a way as to bring the staff closer to the unemployed worker, with the result that the civil servant dealing with a case is better able to understand the worker's claim and the worker, for his part, has an opportunity to understand the act better. This humanization process will probably lead to fewer abuses.
In this program there are, of course, bound to be weaknesses and abuses, but there is not one government program or area of public policy of which I am aware in which no abuses occur. I was in business myself. I used to meet a lot of businessmen and I know how they can arrange quite legally, to avoid all sorts of taxes. Why is it so bad for poor people? Why is it so bad if a person does abuse the unemployment insurance program, when others are allowed to go unchecked just because they have a better education and a different life? The UIC was established by a Liberal government because it saw the need for social justice, because the labour movement has failed to protect poor workers. Any review of the work of the UIC had better not detract from that concept of social justice. As I say, this measure was not brought in at a time when we had to bow to pressure from the New Democratic Party: it was at a time when we enjoyed a majority in this House.
Last year there was a lot of talk about Bill C-125. That bill was brought down by the government as a measure of the concern for some of the abuses to which attention had been called. The reason the bill did not move through all stages was not simply because of opposition from the NDP. It is probably a good principle to say that workers leaving their jobs without just cause should not receive unemployment insurance, but there is no way in which this principle can be administered before we are sure that humanization and decentralization of the administration has been tested thoroughly. We must make sure that people are not judged by a civil servant who is 100 miles away.
In addition, we must drastically change the appeal procedures. More appeal committees are required in rural areas and small communities so that decisions are made in a humane way. I conclude by saying that this review had better not retract from the concept of social justice from which the legislation was born.

Mr. Speaker, it is certainly a pleasure for me to join with other members in the final stages of this throne speech debate. I should like to preface my remarks by extending my best wishes to His Excellency the Governor General and Madame Leger. He has already made his mark felt in the Canadian fabric, and I am sure all Canadians look forward to seeing His Excel-

lency and his wife in the near future as they begin their tour across the provinces of this great country.
I should also like to pay tribute to that great statesman who will be sadly missed, not only here in Ottawa but indeed all across this country, the Hon. Roland Michener, a great man who has reached into the hearts of all Canadians. To him and his wife I wish many joyous years in their new life. Congratulations should also be extended to the mover and the seconder of the address in reply to the Speech from the Throne.
In the past week a great deal of criticism has been levelled at the government by many members of this House for the failure that it displayed so remarkably during the past session. To me, this Speech from the Throne sounds no different from others I have heard and read. In particular, it has a very familiar ring; it reminds me of that given a year ago. Speeches produced as of late by the office of the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) for such occasions always sound dull, dead and full of the same old promises and hints that the government is taking the wishes and desires of the people and the provinces into consideration.
The Prime Minister has described the throne speech as a matter of fact program setting out the intentions and the priorities of the government in this second session of the twenty-ninth parliament. It is a matter of fact speech in that the government has forgotten, or just plain refused to deal with, the important issues that face Canadians today. One of the greatest issues, of course, as one only need ask any Canadian, is inflation, not the so-called energy crisis. Another is the spiralling cost of goods and extreme shortages, particularly shortages in the construction and building industry at the present time. It is obvious that the government has tried to buy time by hiding the facts from the people.
As much of the press and news media to the south of us say, if you give the people a new crisis or problem it will take their minds off the real problem. This is why the minority government has leaped at the opportunity to use the energy crisis as a cover-up. What does the government want to cover up? Obviously, the one thing it did not want to acknowledge was the cancerous effect that inflation was having on the health of the economy of this country. Inflation has turned those on fixed incomes into nothing better than beggars who are reliant upon the few crumbs that this government saw fit to throw in their direction last year. Inflation has been blamed on worldwide problems such as the United States economy, even the Zulu problem in Africa. In other words, Mr. Speaker, everyone has become the scapegoat instead of the goat, which in this case is this government and its partner in the coalition that we have seen in the House during the past year.
This throne speech has been termed by many hon. members a complete and absolute failure. It has failed to provide a means for halting the inflationary spiral that my party has been warning of for months. It has failed to give hope to the people of this country. Instead, it has given them the story that we will have to put up with it for a little bit longer. Many people have noticed the mild form of brainwashing that has been going on in recent weeks in press releases and statements made on behalf of the government. First we were told that the economy of Canada
March 11, 1974

was growing at a fast rate. Then we were told that it was growing even faster than the rate of most other countries. Then we were told that we could afford to suffer more because we had had it so good up until now. It all adds up to one thing, Mr. Speaker, and that is that the worst is yet to come.
Last Thursday the right hon. member for Prince Albert (Mr. Diefenbaker) who made, as always, an eloquent speech in the House, presented a detailed analysis of the actual rate of inflation that has been experienced in Canada in recent years. As he pointed out, in 1971 the Prime Minister said that inflation was licked, that we in this country had beaten it. This, of course, was at the expense of the workers; we experienced the greatest rate of unemployment we have ever known in recent years.
In 1971, inflation began at the mild rate of 1.6 per cent. By the end of the year it had risen to 5 per cent, and so on until at the end of 1973 it had reached the rate of 9.1 per cent. These figures reflect the government's attitude to government: it is a group of people who are reluctant to act, each relying on the other to prop up the boat. In other words, the boat is out of control and we can all expect to be floundering in the future under the ineptness that this government has displayed.
Today Canada is beset with deep-rooted and chronic problems. It is up to us to decide whether we want to cure those problems or to sit by and do nothing about them. There are many signs in Canada today that unemployment will continue to rise in some regions of this country, while in others, such as my own area, labour shortages will exist. There will be further price increases, creating more social inequities and requiring more government expenditure, resulting in even greater inflation. We have a serious economic problem, and if we are to survive something must be done about it.
One thing that a government must not do is to put forward the proposition that we sit idly by and do nothing. But this government's policy seems to be to sit and wait, hoping that the inflationary forces will go away and that things will work out all right in the end. This is the road to disaster. There has to be a recognition of the responsibility to maintain price stability. To pursue the government's present course of action, to take more of what we have had already-which is really what the throne speech promises-will lead to higher inflation, greater increases in prices and more frustration for those unable to meet those prices.
The list of failures one can draw out of the throne speech evidences the lack of mention of any of today's important subjects. For example, there was no mention of a planned reduction in or elimination of the federal sales tax on all clothing and building materials. Why not? There was no mention of the program of the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Lalonde) to consult and negotiate with his provincial counterparts to lower the age of eligibility for old age pensioners to 60 from 65, either on a voluntary basis or on a year by year basis.
No mention was made of any inquiries into profits from oil, intercity rapid transit and a host of other items needing legislation. No provision has been made for a full inquiry into the Unemployment Insurance Act and the way the commission has been administered. The govern-
The Address-Mr. Wise
ment has failed to deal adequately with the acute shortage of farm labour. If there were provision for the same number of farm labourers as there are government employees hired to administer the schemes and many plans that exist today, there would be no difficulty in this area and Canadian farmers would not have to scrounge all over the world in an effort to find workers to harvest crops.
Too many people find it more profitable to collect unemployment insurance benefits, and the benefits of other schemes, than to work. Others who work and receive less than those on unemployment insurance and other government schemes are understandably dejected. It is an undeniable fact of human nature that an individual is happier when he or she is productive. Human beings cannot be content for too long without achieving, without striving, whatever their goal or the end result. Just being, without doing, runs counter to human nature and to history. Therefore, the man who wants to work but cannot feels deceived and rejected.
Perhaps the most serious consequence of all this is that people who have lost their incentive to work and to succeed have lost faith in themselves and their government. The first is disastrous, but the second, of course, is understandable. This is a tragedy beyond description. It is particularly a tragedy for a young country which has so much in the way of human and material resources, a country which should be on the threshold of its greatest era.
This is the path down which this government is leading us. So preoccupied is it with its so-called crisis of the moment, so preoccupied is it with its lust for power that it is blind to the course of events which, I am sad to say, is not unfolding as it should be. Recent figures released by Statistics Canada show that the consumer price index is reaching ever higher points. In fact, it was only a few months ago that we saw the highest percentage increase in almost 30 years. Although these trends have been forecast, it is still depressing to have the cold reality verified by statistics. To me, it seems inevitable that if we remain on our present course Canada will suffer economic chaos and disaster.
It is the bread and butter issues that make Canada, and it is the bread and butter issues that are foremost in the minds of the people. It is the things that affect bread and butter issues that should be examined, if we are to resolve our problems. Canada's problems on the domestic front will not be resolved by spending hundreds of thousands of dollars in financing groups to overthrow the white regime in Africa. Our problems will not be solved by the spending of hundreds of thousands of dollars on metal abortions called sculptures, while people live at or below the poverty line. Our problems will not be solved by wasting money in refurnishing government offices at high cost, or by having the plants inside public service buildings changed every few months.
We in Canada require a new, imaginative and different economic policy. We need a policy that will embrace the future in security for all Canadians-the old, the young, the French, the English and the new Canadian, as well as the poor and the not so poor. No other objective is appro-
392

March 11, 1974
The Address-Mr. Penner
priate for Canada than the objective of making a nation that is truly great. That objective, I submit, has been missed by this minority government.

Mr. Speaker, during the recess of parliament, my colleagues and I from northern Ontario travelled rather extensively throughout that vast region which extends from the Manitoba boundary to the boundary of Quebec. Incidentally, that huge region of which I speak is much more than the hinterland of Toronto. It is also something greater than the underdeveloped backyard of Ontario. Northern Ontario in itself is, and must continue to be considered by the federal government as one of the major economic and geographic regions of this country.
During our tour, my fellow members of parliament and myself sensed a new attitude of optimism among the people who inhabit this region. Far from feeling neglected and forgotten, these citizens of Canada now see that the future is on their side and that greater prosperity and economic development is on the verge of being theirs.

speakerposition: Deputy House Leader of the Official Opposition; Progressive Conservative Party Deputy House Leader
speechtext: The Davis government is on their side.

The Davis government has just recently discovered northern Ontario, as indicated in their Speech from the Throne. It has paid lip service to the region but we in northern Ontario are not fooled by that, and that is why we have not elected any Tories to the House of Commons from our region.
In this world of serious shortages, we in northern Ontario possess a great deal of what is needed and what is in increasing demand throughout the world, including pulp, paper and paper products, lumber, iron, copper, lead, zinc, gold, freshwater fish, wilderness areas for recreation, and breathtaking natural beauty to satisfy the eye of the most discriminating artist. It is even suggested by some that before too long we may be producing oil from wells located near the shores of Hudson Bay.
Facing all this development as we are, we are also confronted with a serious difficulty, namely, the need for an adequate labour force to bring on-stream the resources which we have and which the world needs. Strenuous efforts are urgently demanded to attract many thousands of new people into northern Ontario to work in the mines, the mills and the forests of this region. Much of the work is hard and we require a hearty breed of people who are physically fit and who during their time off are able to enjoy and find satisfaction in outdoor recreation such as skiing, skidooing, fishing, hunting, boating and hiking. To bring these people from the congested cities of this land and from overcrowded countries abroad, we must make available to them a number of basic requirements, including adequate housing, of course, essential community services such as sewage treatment, water, health care and recreational facilities including radio and television communication. Many communities in my constituency badly need upgraded facilities for recreation in addition to that which is offered by the outdoors itself.
We are very pleased with the announcement by the Secretary of State (Mr. Faulkner) that additional funds will be provided the CBC for its so-called "accelerated coverage plan." It may surprise some hon. members of this

House to learn that while city dwellers have multi-channel television, there are communities in northwestern Ontario still lacking even the basic radio-television services provided elsewhere by the CBC. Pressure is also continuously being exerted on Bell Canada to expand and upgrade telephone communications in remote areas of sparse population. The capital cost of these projects is immense, but we do not apologize for one moment in expecting people in Canada who already have these services to help us and to share the cost. After all, we have provided much of the natural wealth which has helped to make possible the very high standard of living enjoyed elsewhere in Canada and now we are asking for some return.
It has long been the practice in this country to extend certain tax advantages to those companies engaged in resource development, particularly mining. This system was altered to some considerable extent by the federal government's tax reforms and most provinces are now. making changes also to reduce these tax privileges. Be that as it may, one possible solution to the manpower shortage in the resource sector, which has never been applied in Canada to my knowledge, would be the offer of special tax advantages to those who work in the mines, the mills, the forests and on the railroads in our resource regions-those who work hard under certainly less than favourable conditions and those who live in communities which lack many of the amenities which people elsewhere in Canada, particularly in the urban areas, have come to take for granted.
It is one thing to work in air-conditioned offices, with coffee breaks, lunch hours, soft chairs, conference rooms and cafeterias; it is quite another thing to handle a chainsaw all day, operate a heavy drill deep in the earth, or run a deisel locomotive for hundreds of monotonous miles through a tunnel of coniferous trees. If we want the natural resources of this country to be processed and turned into manufactured goods for our use and for export, and if we want to provide the liquid wealth for business and investment-and I am sure we do-then we must give extra consideration to those who work so hard in developing these resources. They must be well paid, better paid than most, I suggest. They must be given improved housing, health care and recreational facilities. In addition, it seems to me we should consider that an extra tax exemption is due to the workers of this country who produce our natural wealth. We now give special consideration to those in business. The previous speaker mentioned the way in which people in business are able to use the tax laws to their benefit. I argue that those who dig the ore and cut the trees need, and deserve, a special resource-developer exemption of at least $1,000 per year. This will, of course, cause some bureaucratic outcries to the effect that such a proposal is complicated and may be difficult to administer. It will be asked, who is a resource developer? There is no doubt that if you drill rock in the damp and dust of a mine, you are a resource-developer; or if you handle a chain-saw in the forests of this land in all kinds of weather, you are a resource-developer. Because of the difficult nature of their work, less of what these resource-developers earn should be destined for the government treasuries of this land.

The time is brief for participation in this debate, but before concluding I should like to make a few comments about our railroads. The railway companies of this country certainly need a vigorous shaking up. Employee morale on the CPR is appallingly low. Although morale is somewhat better on the CNR, it still leaves much to be desired. Those in the running trades on the CNR, for example, are terribly overworked and fatigued. They put the maximum number of trains through the railway towns of northern Ontario. In the very midst of this situation, the CNR and the Brotherhood of Locomotive Engineers have conspired together-there is no other word for it-to force upon the CNR engineers in Nakina and Hornepayne, Ontario, a run-through proposal which involves extra miles, longer hours, more time away from home, further fatigue and an additional threat to safety.
Tomorrow morning a meeting is scheduled with a union representative and officials of the Department of Labour to make a plea for a moratorium on this run-through proposal. We will also ask for an inquiry in the town of Hornepayne with the workers who will be affected. We hope that during our discussion tomorrow the union leader will remember that to call another man "brother" means to act in his interest, to defend his rights and to be concerned about his well-being, rather than to work in concert with the company to initiate change in the name of efficiency, which seldom proves to be the case and which only imposes new hardships on these men.
During the life of this parliament, and no doubt in the next one, more and more attention will be paid to the natural resources of Canada which we possess in such abundance. New policies will be required to guarantee a continuity of supply, more processing in Canada and better communities located in our resource regions. Certainly, as I have indicated in my brief remarks, fresh incentives are needed for the worker who performs the hard labour in order to raise still further the standard of living for Canadians wherever they live.

Mr. Speaker, first I should like to compliment the mover and the seconder of the address in reply to the Speech from the Throne. Also, I echo the best wishes of other members to His Excellency the Governor General upon his appointment. While I have nice words to say, I should like to compliment the Minister of State for Urban Affairs (Mr. Basford) for finally realizing that the shortage of serviced land has created the enormous problem-which exists in respect of housing in this country. He referred, unfortunately only in minor detail, to the proposal made by members on this side of the House and adopted, so to speak, our suggestion that this government has a responsibility to use its funding, its power over the money supply of this country, to make it possible that efficient land be available for building.
A deathbed conversion.

It certainly is a deathbed conversion, but finally, once again, this government has adopted policies proposed on this side of the House.
I was also pleased to hear the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) say that he intended to get tough with the big
The Address-Mr. Blenkarn
guys big business, big labour and big government. I am surprised that he did not speak to the parliamentary secretary from the riding of Gloucester and advise him that that essentially is the basis of an incomes policy. It is unfortunate that the party which governs this country cannot understand economics.
However, what I really wish to speak about today is the inordinate cost of housing and, in particular, housing land. It is unfortunate that the Minister of State for Urban Affairs is not here. When I spoke on the question of housing costs and housing lot costs in the debate last year, the price of a lot for a single family house in my city of Mississauga was about $20,000. Unfortunately, I must report to the House that because this government has done nothing about the cost of housing land, and because it has allowed inflation in respect of housing to run rampant, the cost of a single family lot in Mississauga-not just one, but 90 lots in a subdivision; and not an ideal lot or subdivision but one which backs on the Queen Elizabeth Highway, with all its noise has been negotiated for $42,500, an increase of well over 100 per cent in one year.
Mr. Speaker, May I call it six o'clock?
