Mr. Speaker, before the supper adjournment I stated that land prices, indeed house prices in my constituency certainly and also across the country, were disastrously high a year ago for a young family wanting to buy their first house. To describe them as disastrously high today would not even begin adequately to describe the problem. A year ago the Urban Development Institute indicated that possibly no more than 5 per cent of families could afford to purchase a new house with the minimal down payment required to cover the financing. I suggest to you, sir, that even though we have the increases in wages this year, under no circumstances can any but a very few young people raising a family begin to contemplate the purchase of their own house.
As I said before supper, I welcome the indication by the minister that he is prepared to do something about serviced land. There is an old political saying that members of the opposition often use: too little, too late. With prices of housing rising today at an unprecedented rate, it is certainly too little, too late. Presumably one of the problems is the fact that this government continues to rely on Statistics Canada for an indication of housing costs. I would like to remind them that Statistics Canada, in determining housing costs, is not referring at all to new houses prices; it is referring to the cost of maintenance of housing. To most of us, the cost of keeping our house does not increase because we have an existing mortgage or an existing lease on an apartment, so Statistics Canada does not really reflect the enormous escalation in costs. It may refer to heating costs increasing, it may refer to electricity

March 11, 1974
The Address-Mr. Blenkarn
costs increasing, or to some increases in interest rates, but those increases are only a bag of shells compared with the real costs for those wanting to enter the housing market, for those who have no home, who have a new family and who want to get started in life.
In Toronto alone the average price of a house sold under the multiple listing service last year increased by $9,000. I doubt that there are many members of this House who, relying on the salaries paid here, and even if their wives are working, would be able to save in one year $9,000 after payment of taxes. That is the extent of the increase. It boils down to this fact, that those who have been trying to get a few dollars together to buy a house suddenly see the cost of that house going up and up.
I can say to you, sir, that in my city of Mississauga the price of a house is increasing at the rate of nearly $2,000 a month. When I asked the minister last Friday what he was going to do, and did he realize that the price of every house was going up at the rate of $50 a day, seven days a week including Sundays, the minister said something about social housing and he mentioned the Speech from the Throne. I say that the Minister of State for Urban Affairs and this government have no concept of the social damage they are causing in condemning forever most young families and their children to wandering in apartment corridors or using apartment parking lots for playgrounds. That is the policy of this government. They are not really concerned about what in fact is happening. They rely on Statistics Canada and say that the cost of housing went up 7 per cent or 8 per cent. That is not the case at all. Perhaps for the average person it did go up by only that amount, but for those who have young families to raise the cost of housing has become prohibitive. Yet my friends to my left continue to support this excuse for a government.
We in this party welcome the government's suggestion that it will support urban transit. There are now arrangements for service on both the CNR line running through my constituency and the CPR line servicing Streetsville and the centre parts of Mississauga. That rail line could well support commuter service. This boils down to the whole question of servicing, because the Speech from the Throne seems to suggest the minister thinks that just increasing sewage assistance programs would be an answer to the problem of the cost of servicing. Surely by now the minister realizes that urban transit, parks and water service are an integral part of making serviced land available so that houses can be built. Surely the minister realizes that just increasing sewage assistance programs is not enough. Although it is welcome, it is just not enough. As I have said, it is too little, too late. In fact, it is very much too little, and in many cases very much too late.
That brings me to the very serious problem now confronting this country. To a large extent it was set out by the hon. member for Don Valley (Mr. Gillies) when he spoke earlier in this debate. He suggested that we have a housing problem, but that housing problems cannot be solved in the inflationary climate that exists. So long as prices continue to escalate, this government's answer seems to be more social housing. Pretty soon they will have people earning $20,000 a year qualifying for social housing.
Hear, hear!
These people would have everybody in blue jeans.
The Governor General and the Prime Minister live in social housing.

One of the major problems is that people throughout this nation have no confidence in paper money because this government has no confidence. This government has no intention of stepping in with an incomes policy or with a commodities policy. I am glad the President of the Treasury Board (Mr. Drury) is here, because I was after him earlier today. He said that what I said was rhetoric, but look at the way he produces blue books. The only increase in size is, not physically but in the size of the figures at the bottom of the pages. Billions of dollars are allocated by this government for one expenditure after another, and the cost of government grows and grows like a snowball rolling down a hill. Surely in a government that was concerned about people there would be some control over government expenditures, but the money supply has been increased by 50 per cent or 60 per cent in three years.
People in this country have no confidence in paper money: witness the lines in banks to buy gold and silver; witness the price of Olympic coins and their shortage. People with no confidence in paper money are rushing into the housing field to buy residential housing; they feel that real estate will protect them and their savings against the ravages of inflation. Housing is already in short supply, but the price is being pushed up by one speculator vying with another. "Every man for himself" is all this government talks about. The message is, "Protect yourself against inflation in this country, because Trudeau's gang is not going to help you". That is fine for the rich and for the privileged, because they have the credit with which to buy real estate; they can get a bank loan or go to a mortgage company and get a mortgage loan. They can buy and bid up the price. You fellows would like to continue to support them because you really do not believe in the ordinary fellow; you believe in the privileged groups such as the big unions.
That is exactly the kind of attitude of this government and its lackeys to my left. They really do not care about the ordinary person. This government does not care about organizing and using its powers over banking and financing to make sure the banks will no longer advance money directly or indirectly on second mortgages. It does not care that trust companies and loan companies will continue to use the sale price as the valuation price, even though the value of the bricks and mortar represents less than one-third of the total price in many cases; even though most of the value is in land, and land values are bid up; even though all sorts of people who need housing compete with speculators, real estate agents and lawyers. Those who have the bucks in their pockets and the credit allowed by the banking system, which should be under the control of the Minister of Finance, continue to finance speculators.
Let me tell you a couple of stories, Mr. Speaker. One of my senior employees bought a house the other day that
March 11, 1974

was listed at $79,000. Before he bought the house he heard that three or four other offers had been made, so instead of bidding the list price he bid $81,000. He was lucky; he got it by bidding $250 higher than anyone else.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Order, please. I regret to interrupt the hon. member, but the time allotted to him by the rather exact rules decided upon today has expired.

Mr. Speaker, recently there has been some publicity about a private member's bill that I introduced which calls upon this House to have a committee formed to examine the request that has come to Canada from the council of the Turks and Caicos Islands for a closer relationship with this country. The press coverage on this matter has been very large. From the smallest to the largest newspaper in Canada the idea has been examined. It has been covered by radio and by both national television networks. The story of the islanders wanting to join Canada has taken on a life of its own away and beyond my advocacy in putting it forward and many people have become interested in the idea.
Would you like to be the first governor?
I would not mind.
I thought you were looking for a job.

I have not seen an idea capture the imagination of the public to the extent that this one has, during my years in parliament. It is not that this is the most serious problem facing Canada and deserves priority, because Canada has many weighty problems to deal with. We heard of those problems in the Speech from the Throne. But in some ways the idea of these islands is a relief to Canadians from the discussions of inflation, housing, employment and all the other great issues in this country. This is nevertheless an important idea, Mr. Speaker, and many people in Canada want it examined. My office has received hundreds and hundreds of letters urging me to continue bringing the matter before the parliament of Canada and enlisting the support of the members of this chamber.
The idea has developed from the initial reaction of newspapers taking a sort of humorous view of it, as a kind of winter madness thing that seizes a member of parliament. Reaction has ranged from the idea that I was seeking publicity in bringing this matter before the country, to the idea that after nine years parliament is finally getting to me: "The man is off his rocker even to be thinking about things like that". I hope neither of those two extreme views is true, Mr. Speaker, because I have been serious about this matter from the very beginning. It is not the sort of thing that one plays around with. One does not play with the emotions of a group of people who have made a serious request to this country. I am asking the Canadian government and the House of Commons to respect the sincere petition that has come to this country to examine the idea of a closer relationship.
Basically, what I want to do in the few minutes available to me tonight-because there is not enough time to go into detail-is deal with essentially the attitude that has emanated from the government and which presumably is
The Address-Mr. Saltsmcm
the position of the Department of External Affairs as expressed by the minister. First of all, they do not want to hear anything about it; they want it to go away. They do not even want to examine the idea, and they certainly do not want to discuss it. I can understand that there are some serious issues involved in a closer relationship with a group of islands in the Caribbean regardless of how well intentioned the islands, or myself or others advocating the idea may be. It means that we would have to examine our foreign policy in the Caribbean. You cannot just talk about whether 6,000 people in the islands are going to come into Canada as if that is the end of it. It has repercussions on our foreign policy in the Caribbean and our relationship with other countries there, and their future.
If these islands were to come into some kind of closer union, they would receive benefits from this country and we would receive benefits from them. Other countries in the Caribbean might then make the same request to the Canadian government and we would have to decide what our foreign policy would be. So I am not discounting the fact that the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Sharp) has a perfect right to be wary of a proposal of this kind and to consider its seriousness.
It is also very obvious that if the Turks and Caicos Islands were to come into Canada in one form or another, they would probably be better off than other countries in the Caribbean with the repercussions that flow from such a situation. It would also mean that Canada would be challenging the United States in the Caribbean. The United States dominates the Caribbean in commercial matters because of the port facilities in Florida. If we were, by taking in these islands, to become part of the Caribbean, we could challenge the commercial supremacy of the United States in that area. It also means we would be willing to accept black people into confederation in the same way as we have accepted white people.
When I talk about the Turks and Caicos Islands becoming part of Canada, people say, "That is pretty well impossible. It cannot happen". I always respond by saying, "Why not?" If Newfoundland became part of Canada, why cannot these islands become part of Canada? They are closer to Ottawa than British Columbia. So distance should be no object. We must decide whether the only people who are eligible to become citizens of this country are white or whether blacks as well are to be eligible.
I do not discount the seriousness of my proposal. I like to think that we in this country have advanced to the point where colour, religion and similar factors do not make any difference and men and women are accepted into our society for what they are. Many can say that; on the other hand, many will say that we have not reached the point at which we are without prejudice and can comfortably assimilate many people of different kinds. That will be the point we shall need to determine. We must ask if we are ready to remove distinctions between people, especially people who are asking to become part of this country.
They are serious about becoming part of Canada, and it is quite proper for the Department of External Affairs to

March 11, 1974
The Address-Mr. Saltsman
raise such issues and to worry about them. However, I object when the Secretary of State for External Affairs raises issues which are less than real and are designed to confuse rather than to clarify the situation. First, the minister talked about a new form of imperialism. He has since modified his position: he no longer talks about imperialism, he talks about colonialism. He said that our action, if we assimilated the islands, might be interpreted as imperialism or colonialism. Why in the world did he make a statement like that? It is not Canada which wants to take the islands in; it is the islanders who have petitioned Canada for they want to become part of this country.
The minister's utterances reflect the views of liberalism. According to modern liberalism, it is fine for such islands to seek independence. We will give them a little foreign aid, pat them on the head and tell them to go their own way, but we want no part of them. Such thinking masquerades as modern thinking. It is all right to atomize the world! I suggest that by taking members of a poorer society into our midst we would be fulfilling our responsibility as a richer society.
The minister talked about building a fence around the islands. Has anybody built a fence around this country? A fence does not keep out the poor. It is our immigration policy which keeps out the peoples of the Caribbean. That is the fence we have built around this country, and if you take the islands in we car>
build it around them, if that is what you want to do. The situation would not be the same as in Grenada: the people in the Turks and Caicos Islands want to belong to Canada.
The minister does not understand the reason for so much unhappiness in the Caribbean. White people give almost nothing to the people in the Caribbean, even though they may invest money and spend time down there as tourists. The real benefits which come to a people do not come from the few jobs you may provide in the tourist season. They come from being part of a society, part of a social structure, part of its wealth. If we want to help people, if we really want to redistribute wealth, we will take them in. If we take them in we may see the beginning of the end of people being pushed around, and perhaps the introduction of a modern form of federalism. Talk of modern federalism is not popular: talk of countries splitting apart seems to be more in vogue.
What bothered me most about the minister's statement was his bland suggestion that we must not raise expectations. How patronizing! We must not raise their expectations. You could almost hear him saying, "After all, they are people who do not have much education. They are not sophisticated. They would not understand." Mr. Speaker, these people are educated, and they do understand. They understand only too well how remote is the possibility of their being taken in. Yet remote though the possibility is, they want to see it debated in this country. They badly want to be part of this country and are willing to take a chance on the acceptance of this idea.
I can almost hear the minister saying what was said 20 or 30 years ago about programs like medicare. Some said, "We must not talk about medicare. It will raise the expectations of people, expectations which can never be satisfied. You must not talk about old age pensions of $35 or

$40 per month. You would only raise expectations. The poor will be upset because they cannot get such a pension and we cannot afford to give it to them."
That is exactly what Paul Martin said.

When you do not want to do something, you can always say that talking about it will raise expectations. Bringing forward this subject has laid a heavy responsibility upon me. I am fully aware of it. The alternative was to do nothing. It seems to me that what has been happening in the Turks and Caicos Islands is unique. It offers us a challenge to which we can respond. The danger of raising expectations must be faced, in the hope that we can provide a better future for the people in the islands and bring a new and beautiful area into Canada.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am happy to have the opportunity to speak in this debate and to extend my congratulations to the mover and the seconder of the address in reply to the Speech from the Throne, the hon. member for Spadina (Mr. Stollery) and the hon. member for Sherbrooke (Mr. Pelletier). They are typical of the young, vigorous, knowledgeable and enthusiastic people who come to parliament. That is why this is such a dynamic place wherein so many things happen. I congratulate both hon. members on their speeches. Both members are bilingual. Even though they come from different types of ridings they display the same esprit de corps and the same enthusiasm for their work here. I also extend my best wishes and the best wishes of Algoma riding to our new Governor General and Madame Leger. We wish them well in discharging their new responsibilities as representatives of our country.
Perhaps more interesting than anything else has been the change in attitude of the opposition that we have seen in this parliament since the last speech from the throne was debated. The first session of the twenty-ninth parliament opened on January 4, 1973, with the opposition practically sitting on the edge of their seats waiting to move across the aisle to become the government. We do not see that kind of anticipation or expectation now. We do not hear them saying, "Within the next couple of months or so, when we take over the government of this country . . . " It is very understandable why they now have reduced enthusiasm and expectation. Their whole outlook has really dampened because of the progress made in the first session of the twenty-ninth parliament.
That session was one of the most productive sessions of parliament in many years. Over 50 pieces of legislation were passed. All of the major commitments for legislation outlined in the Speech from the Throne were carried out in that session, including many important items. The energy debate and the debate on legislation concerning privacy and wiretapping seemed to dominate the scene during the last two or three months of the fall session.
However, when historians write the pages of history for the first session of the twenty-ninth parliament they will find it significant because of the very many important pieces of social legislation that were passed. I think of the family allowance bill which increased family allowances
March 11, 1974

from $7.21 a month on average to $20 a month on average across the country. I think of the significant changes that were made in the old age security system, both the universal old age security pension and the guaranteed income supplement, and the fact that even though we previously tied this to cost of living increases, it was accelerated to become effective quarterly if there were increases in the cost of living.
I think of the changes that were made to the Canada Pension Plan to remove the 2 per cent ceiling in the benefits of the plan due to inflation. I think of the whole outline of attack on our social problems through the orange paper which the Minister of National Health an Welfare (Mr. Lalonde) brought forward in the spring of 1973. Much progress was made in the discussions with the provincial premiers on this policy, and more is to come. Certainly during 1973 the biggest and most expensive items were adopted as legislation by this House. Many pieces of legislation and policies adopted by the government were to counteract the effects of inflation on those who cannot protect themselves, people in the low income brackets and pensioners.
I think, also, of the assistance provided in respect of food prices, such as the subsidy on bread. A long-term agreement was made with the Canadian Wheat Board to ensure a stable price in the cost of flour over a seven-year period, combined with a subsidy not only to give the wheat producers a stable price for the next seven years but to give stability to this essential item in the diet of Canadians. I think of the consumer subsidy for milk. The government took action to control the increase which was inevitable in regard to oil produced in our country when world prices rose rapidly. I believe the 1973 session was very productive. I am confident that the session now beginning will be equally productive.
The Speech from the Throne refers to maintaining high levels of income, production and employment to increase the supply of food and other commodities. It refers to increasing the production of our country so that we may produce as many new jobs this year as in 1973. In his budget speech in the spring of 1973, the Minister of Finance (Mr. Turner) very modestly talked about creating at least 300,000 new jobs. By the end of the year over 430,000 new jobs were created in Canada, a record for this country. This is certainly the kind of fiscal and monetary policy which we need in a country whose work force will increase by 50 per cent from 1965 to 1980. There can be no doubt that with this continued increase in our economy there will also be more jobs in 1974.
There is also reference in the Speech from the Throne to protecting people from the effects of inflation by programs which were implemented in 1973. These were designed to help those on fixed incomes and large families through family allowance benefits and increases in veterans pensions of some 25 per cent. These programs were all implemented in the 1973 session of this parliament. Likewise, the government has acted to cushion increases in prices to consumers. I refer to the action that was taken relating to oil prices and subsidies on essentials such as bread and milk.
In his speech on December 6 the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) gave the initial outline of a national energy
The Address-Mr. Foster
policy; a plan to have one price for the whole country, a plan to be self-sufficient later in this decade by the construction of a pipeline, and the use of some of the export tax revenues to ensure that the price of oil in eastern Canada will be at reasonable levels. Perhaps one of the most important thrusts of the Speech from the Throne is the plan to ensure adequate supplies and production of food. To do this it is proposed to place many bills before the House in this session which will ensure there is a fair price for the consumer and a reasonable return for the producer.
It is planned to place a bill before the House relating to the Agricultural Stabilization Act to ensure that producers can produce their products and that if there are large-scale fluctuations in the producers' price, they will be protected. There will be changes in respect of advance payments. In the past we have had a scheme of farm stored produce on which advances could be made. This will be extended. I understand the limits will be raised in all parts of Canada.
The Speech from the Throne also refers to improved assistance to encourage young men to go into farming. This is very important. During the recess I attended a conference in Ottawa on the need for farm labour. This problem is being faced right across our country. At an earlier time farmers could perhaps run a simple operation without much help other than from the family. However, as the family grows up and moves away, and as farm units become larger, there is a greater need for hired help.
The conference went on to discuss in detail the measures necessary to encourage more people to work on farms. We also talked about a program being implemented this year by the Department of Manpower to establish farm labour pools especially for the assistance of market gardeners and fruit growers who require a large number of people for relatively short periods. Under this scheme, young people and others who wish to enter the labour force for a short period will be transported to countries where the crops are grown in an effort to overcome the labour difficulties faced in these areas.
Perhaps no greater problem faces Canadian agriculture today than the shortage of feed grain and its high price.
There is no shortage.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
Certainly, those who produce feed grain are fortunate to receive the price of they do today-possibly three times higher than it has ever been in our history. There is certainly a crunch felt by those producing beef, on the basis of this high-priced grain. I am confident the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Whelan), in his usual capable way, will be coming forward with a solution in the coming days or weeks.
There were one or two items of great interest to my constituents announced in the Speech from the Throne and elsewhere. I refer especially to the announcement by the Minister of Regional Economic Expansion (Mr. Jamieson) that changes are being made in the DREE program under which incentives are given to industry to locate in slow-growth areas. Under the new program, smaller enterprises are now able to qualify for assistance. The minimum limit has been lowered from $60,000 to $25,000 or five

March 11, 1974
The Address-Mr. Reynolds
jobs, whichever applies. In November, 1973, a development seminar was held in my constituency and the Minister of Regional Economic Expansion was the keynote speaker. The question of the size of the enterprise which would be eligible for a grant was raised on that occasion.
In conclusion, Mr. Speaker, we on this side of the House are not so naive as to believe we have no problems to face in this second session of the twenty-ninth parliament, nor do we fail to understand their depth and the difficulties in finding solutions to them. But I ask the members of this House, "Would you be willing to trade these difficulties and the material and human resources which we have to deal with them with those of any other country in the world-Britain, United States, West Germany, you name it?" Not one person here would be willing to make such a trade. So let us not pay too much attention to the negative, carping criticism of the opposition. Let us not adopt stupid simplistic solutions such as the wage and price freeze which the Conservatives have advocated and which have failed in other countries.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Order. I am sorry to interrupt the hon. member, but the time allotted to him has expired.

Mr. Speaker, let me first pass on to the new Governor General my best wishes and those of the people of my constituency. I wish him well and I wish his good lady well as they enter their first year of office.

I also wish to congratulate the hon. member for Spadina (Mr. Stollery) and the hon. member for Sherbrooke (Mr. Pelletier) for having replied so brilliantly to the Speech from the Throne.

Why have they had to absorb these large freight rate increases when the people of eastern Canada are asking for equality of oil and gas prices? We have the resources in western Canada, a lot of them in British Columbia, and we are willing to share those resources with the people of eastern Canada. We also want them to help us out on freight rates. We think that this is only fair.
Another issue bothering the people in my riding is the Post Office service. We see some grand advertisements in the newspapers about how the Post Office offers this great one-day service: put your mail in by eleven o'clock and get it delivered the next day, say the advertisements. I see examples all the time where that just is not so. In fact, I asked the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs (Mr. Gray) to investigate the Post Office for false advertising. The people of British Columbia do not know what is happening with their mail. It is not arriving on time. A municipality the size of Delta, with some 65,000 people, has just one post office and that is all. We asked the minister for another one, but the department is not even considering it. The post office in British Columbia is now jokingly called the "royal snail" because it seems to take a very long time to get mail from British Columbia to anywhere in Canada.
Unemployment insurance is another matter that has been bothering the people of British Columbia. As most hon. members who have a constituency office in British Columbia know, their secretaries are receiving about five phone calls a day citing problems with the Unemployment Insurance Commission. These problems are very legitimate. People who deserve to get their unemployment insurance are not receiving it because of some problem within the commission.
The Minister of the Environment (Mr. Davis) said in a speech in his riding about two months ago: "When we go back for the next session this government is going to bring in some strong laws to straighten out this problem". The minister in charge of the Unemployment Insurance Commission said that this was not true. Since then we have had the throne speech and it now appears the government is going to do something about the Unemployment Insurance Commission and manpower.
Why will not this government do what tne Leader of the Official Opposition (Mr. Stanfield) asked, and hold a full inquiry into the Unemployment Insurance Commission so we can find out what is wrong before the government introduces some other program? People within the commission are working very hard at their jobs, but the government is going to disrupt their work with another program which probably will not work any better than the one it had in the past.
Regional economic expansion is another area that bothers the people of British Columbia. In the last election I said that we were not getting our fair share of money; the government said that we were. I put some questions on the order paper and found out that in 1972 the province of Quebec received $66 million. The province of British Columbia received only $650,000. This answer was given by the minister, so I presume the figures are factual. The people of British Columbia do not believe that this is giving them their fair share.
The Address-Mr. Reynolds
The year before that a company by the name of Evans Products opened a mill in Golden, B. C., and received a $2,250,000 grant. They employed 250 people, and everybody thought it was an excellent program. This past year the same type of mill was closed down in the city of Vancouver by Evans Products, which put 250 people out of work. I think this is one area the Department of Regional Economic Expansion should look into and make sure that such things as this do not happen. This is only one example that occurred in British Columbia, but all members of the House know of other examples that parallel this one.
Information Canada has also been an issue in the city of Vancouver. This government opened a beautiful office at the corner of Granville and Robson Streets. There was a bit of an uproar in the city when people found out that they paid $11.67 a square foot in the building they leased for both the first and second floors. After an investigation the people were told that other people were renting space in the same city block for between $2.50 and $5.50 a square foot on the second floor, and that $5.50 was the maximum price that anybody else paid. Yet, as I say, this government was paying $11.67. On the first floor in that block, people were paying anywhere from $6.50 to $11.50 a square foot.
The value of the building that the government leased was $550,000. When the government took a five-year lease from the firm that leased the building to them for $126,000 a year for the first year, building up to $156,000 for the fifth year, it increased the value of the building to over $1 million. I think the people of Canada deserve a better answer than the one the government has given them to date as to exactly why they paid so much money for this building, and who decided that the building would be leased instead of bought, since the building was for sale a few months before the government leased it.
I should like to touch for a moment on housing. This is a problem in my riding where there has been such a startling increase in population. The government says it has done a lot of things to help housing, but what are the things the government has not done? Firstly, it has not removed the sales tax on building materials. This adds to the cost of every home and apartment in this land. The government has eliminated tax incentives for investors in apartment buildings. As a result, apartment buildings are now 99.5 per cent full in Vancouver and just about equally full in other parts of the country.
The NDP government of British Columbia froze land development and automatically land prices skyrocketed. If the government would only let free enterprise build houses without government interference, there would be plenty of housing in Canada and prices would be reasonable. We have only seen a large increase in the price of housing during the last couple of years because the government has been interfering. I have a clipping advertising houses in Houston, Texas. A 1,700-square foot home there sells for $22,900. If houses at this price can be built down there, they can be built here in Canada. But the cost of housing in Canada has increased as a result of government interference at all levels. The federal government must take the biggest share of the blame because of its sales tax on building materials and its elimination of tax incentives for people who invest in housing.

March 11, 1974
The Address-Mr. A. Lambert
I should now like to say a few words about penitentiaries. We have a large penitentiary situated in our area. I give the present minister a lot of credit for what he is doing in our penitentiaries, but I question some of his decisions, such as hiring three people with a Master's degree to go into the British Columbia penitentiary to work in the recreational area and looking for two more. They are not promoting the people who have been working in the penitentiary for years. They are not giving them the opportunity to take further education to increase their own abilities so they can get ahead in their jobs.
Why do we need five professional people in recreation in the British Columbia penitentiary, serving a population of 600 people, when the city of New Westminster and the city of Delta cannot afford to hire that many people? Why does this government not invest some money in the youth of the nation? Perhaps then we will not have so many people in our penitentiaries.
I should like to close, Mr. Speaker, by mentioning an issue that has been given prominence in our area. I refer to price fixing among seven major cement companies in British Columbia. These seven companies were accused of, and pleaded guilty to, conspiring to prevent or lessen competition and were fined a total of $433,000, the largest fine ever imposed under the Combines Investigation Act.
I think there are some questions that have to be asked about this matter. We must remember that Jimmy Sinclair, a former cabinet minister in the party of the government sitting across from us here, was president of Lafarge Cement, one of the seven companies. The late Frank Ross was chairman of the board of Lafarge Cement, and he also had a close relationship with one of those across the floor. We must also remember that when the charges were laid, the minister of justice at the time who was in charge of the investigation was quickly shifted from that portfolio to another. The present minister of housing and urban affairs was also shifted into his present portfolio pretty quickly from consumer affairs.
Why did these things happen, Mr. Speaker? I think that question needs to be answered by this government. Why did these companies plead guilty so quickly? Why did not some of them go to court and try and fight this charge? I think they are just trying to hide something and that this government should have an inquiry made into price fixing in British Columbia.
It is of interest to note that after these charges were made and these firms pleaded guilty, on January 1 of this year Ocean Cement and Lafarge Cement increased their prices again by the same amount. Then on March 1, Lafarge and Ocean Cement increased their prices yet again by the same amount. So these companies are still up to their same old tricks. They have paid the largest fine ever imposed in Canada. In view of the connection of these companies with members of the Liberal government across the way, I think the Canadian people deserve an inquiry into price fixing and that this government should hold this inquiry with the utmost haste.

Mr. Speaker, at the beginning of the present session of the 29th Legislature I

owe to myself to participate in the debate on the Address in reply to the Speech from the Throne. First, I wish to congratulate the movers of the Address, the hon. members for Spadina (Mr. Stollery) and the hon. member for Sherbrooke (Mr. Pelletier). It is quite appropriate, in a democratic Parliament, when someone is making a first speech in the House, for his colleagues to congratulate him because they know from their own experience that it is a first step which will allow him later to express himself better and participate more easily in the debates.
Mr. Speaker, I also wish to join my colleagues to congratulate His Excellency the Governor General and Mrs. Leger and extend to them the best wishes of the people from the Bellechasse riding that I represent. I was pleased to see, with many others, the great humility with which the new Governor General has presided over the opening of this second session. I was very pleased to see that the Governor General chose to renounce the traditional dress and that he was really like everyone else, someone who holds his position with a great competency but also with a great humility.
I also wish to say to the Chair how pleased I am that we can continue our work under his humble guidance. I also wish to congratulate the Deputy Speaker and Chairman of Committees of the Whole House (Mr. McCleave), the Deputy Chairman of Committees of the Whole House (Mr. Laniel) and the Assistant Deputy Chairman of Committees of the Whole House (Mr. Boulanger): I wish them all a long and fruitful career in this House.
The first session of the 29th Parliament was quite productive, Mr. Speaker, since many bills furthering the respect of human and family rights were carried in spite of a minority government in the House which shows that even under a minority government, when we do our best, it is possible to provide for our country a more efficient administration that under a majority government. To be convinced, one has only to consider the 28th Parliament and note that a majority government, Mr. Speaker, was unable to increase family allowances. The amount of old age security pensions had also been increased by a ridiculous percentage, contrary to what happened since the beginning of the 29th Parliament. This shows that Canada, even under a majority government, can do more to provide security for the aged, but it nevertheless remains that thanks to the goodwill shown by all, it was possible to implement those material, physical and financial possibilities and ensure to old people a maximum of security.
Mr. Speaker, it is with satisfaction that Canadians see that this minority government is much more responsive to their demands. It is less arrogant and more inclined to accept in a democratic system the rules of a true democracy, those of a government of the people, by the people and for the people. Obviously, there is yet much to be done before it becomes reality because, Mr. Speaker, trusts, multinational corporations and financial powers still have a strong hold on the government through their contributions to the treasuries of traditional parties.
To be convinced, one only has to consider the goings-on in the oil, sugar and food industries controlled by big corporations.
Mr. Speaker, the Speech from the Throne is nothing but a conventional procedure still used in Parliament for it
March 11, 1974

does not always reflect the legislative measures that the government intends to have adopted by the House. Indeed, the throne speech of the first session of the 29th legislature announced many more radical measures than what was in fact introduced. On the other hand, Mr. Speaker, the throne speech of the second session of the 29th legislature promises very few measures that would solve the many problems facing the Canadian people, while it is highly possible that this Parliament will be presented numerous bills which have not been mentioned in the speech.
That is why, Mr. Speaker, I say that the Speech from the Throne is part of a parliamentary tradition that we respect, of course, but that we should modernize and adapt to modern times, to the present times, to this century.
So I make the wish that this session will be one of deep reform, particularly in the financial area, so we can finally make financially possible what is physically feasible, and the right hon. Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) gave an affirmative answer last week to my colleague for Champlain (Mr. Matte). I welcome this because formerly, not too many years ago, there was a denial of that suggestion, that possibility to make financially possible what was physically feasible by the people of this country.
However, Mr. Speaker, I accept less than I ever did the fact that a sovereign government, as should be that of Canada, should let its policies in all sectors of the economy of this country be dictated by those who have the privilege to control the economic blood of this nation, that is the real credit of this country, namely the privilege of minting the real credit of this nation which is produced by the over-all activity of its people.
Mr. Speaker, the activity of all those working in this country in any field or branch is the real credit of this country whereas the financial institutions to which I referred earlier are the banking institutions of this country which are governed by the Canadian Bank Act and now have the privilege to mint the credit of this nation, and that is why I say that in 1974 things should no longer happen that way.
We, in this Parliament, should give back to our government sovereignty in that field so it will act as a genuine manager, a genuine steering office, as is done in a co-operative, so that everyone may really benefit from the activities of the members of the Canadian society.
However, Mr. Speaker, I read in the throne speech the wish to submit a measure finally allowing the provinces to have and control a sort of provincial bank, as proposed by the former premiers of Alberta and British Columbia, the hon. Mr. Aberhart and Mr. Bennett. Last week, by the way, the Minister of Finance (Mr. Turner) admitted that this initiative or proposal had been initially taken or made by the former premier of British Columbia, and I do hope that the minister, who is now smiling at me, will continue to benefit from the experience of this politician who still can, although he retired from political life, render many great services to our nation.
I hope that measures to be brought in to this effect will not solely be make-believe ones but sound projects giving to provinces a useful tool which will enable them to financially help municipalities fulfill their task as govern-
The Address-Mr. L. Marchand ments closer to people, by providing for a city or a municipality the essential public services at a cost in line with its paying capacity and with reality.
I would also like, Mr. Speaker, to talk about the young unemployed, educated or not. It has become an acute problem in Canada, a problem in which all serious Canadians as well as any responsible government should be interested in order to bring in a solution before it is too late. This problem of unemployed youth is in my view narrowly related to the difficulties that are facing people from 60 to 65 who have also some serious troubles in seeking employment or still in earning an income giving them financial security until they are 65, when under the present legislation an old age security pension will be paid to them.
Mr. Speaker, the unemployment problem is disturbing since according to a document tabled at the Miscellaneous Estimates Committee following a sitting on November 22, 1973 by the Minister of Manpower and Immigration (Mr. Andras), 47 per cent of Canadian unemployed are aged 24 or less.
The main difficulty of young people in getting on the labour market is their lack of experience, and that is the traditional excuse that employers use in refusing a job to the young people who offer their services, either in the public or private sector.
Mr. Speaker, if more understanding is not shown to these young workers, the country will certainly pay for it. Indeed, instead of taking advantage of the energy of these young people to develop the country and make it more prosperous, we will have to give them a certain amount of security, otherwise we will bear the brunt of their dissatisfaction, and instead of enjoying the effects of their dedication, we will suffer the effects of their frustration instead of benefitting the effects of their devotion. Because of the experience we have acquired, it is our duty as adults to take the necessary steps so that our young may become assets in this country instead of liabilities, as it is much too often unfortunately the case within an economic system which disregards the contribution of the young. We are influenced against our will by a society which is profit-oriented instead of being service-oriented.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: Order, please. I must regretfully interrupt the hon. member, but his time has elapsed.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, at the beginning of my few remarks I should like to congratulate the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) on the appointment of our new Governor General, Mr. Leger. I wish Mr. Leger and Madame Leger godspeed and every good wish as they carry out their very important work on behalf of Canada. I think they are off to a good start. I am sure those of us who attended the ball Their Excellencies held at the opening of this session of parliament appreciated the very fine hospitality shown to us all. I should like to say that Madame Leger is very charming. She has a very difficult role as the wife of the Governor General. It is a very important role. She has that very fine attribute, a good memory. When I met Madame Leger the night of the ball, she told me that she had met me a couple of years ago

March 11, 1974
The Address-Mr. L. Marchand at a dinner held at the National Arts Centre. Her memory is a great attribute, and I believe she will carry out her duties very well.
I also wish to congratulate the mover and the seconder of the address in reply to the Speech from the Throne. I believe both members gave excellent addresses. They conducted themselves very well at the start of our debate on the Speech from the Throne. In 1968 I had the honour to second the address in reply to the Speech from the Throne, and my colleague the hon. member for Madawaska-Vic-toria (Mr. Corbin) was the mover. This is an important honour that is given to members. I know that my constituents of Kamloops-Cariboo at that time very warmly received my nomination by the Prime Minister. I am sure the constituents of these hon. members also appreciate the honour bestowed upon their members.
I am very happy about a number of very important things contained in the Speech from the Throne. Some of the matters worth mentioning have started to unfold. I refer in particular to the legislation in respect of native housing. Mention of this appeared in the Speech from the Throne and later the Minister of State for Urban Affairs (Mr. Basford) announced a very important policy regarding native housing. A number of ingredients contained in this announcement are very important.
First of all, it met almost verbatim the representation made to the government by the Native Council of Canada. The Metis, the native people not under the Indian Act, I believe for a long time have been left out of society. I do not think provincial governments by and large have done a very good job on behalf of the Metis people. These people have come under provincial jurisdiction, and by and large they have been left out of society. In addition, society has tended to leave out the non-treaty Indian people. I think this announcement by the minister is probably one of the most significant statements in respect of housing or any othe matter to be made in a long time by the national or any other government on behalf of the Metis people in this country.
I hope that as progress is made down the road to implementation of this policy the native groups will be consulted more and more and will be used a great deal more in the implementation of the policy. When the announcement was made, I believe it was very warmly received by the president of the Native Council of Canada, Mr. Tony Belcourt. Very often when announcements are made, the native people are skeptical, but that was not the case this time. They said that maybe they were entering a new era.
All too often there is confrontation between native groups and the government, and this is not the way to proceed. There must be consultation between them and understanding, and policies worked out and implemented. I welcome this decision by the minister. I think it is farsighted, and I hope that the provincial governments which have been responsible over the years for the Metis people and the non-status Indians will respond in a very positive manner to the minister's call to them to meet the other part of the policy. If they cannot, then I suppose the minister will perhaps have to look at it again. However, in

all sincerity I call upon the provincial governments throughout the country to respond positively to the needs of the Metis people and the Indians.
I think there is the highest concentration of Metis in the prairie provinces. I believe the province of Alberta has been trying very hard to respond in positive ways to meet the needs of the Metis and Indians. It is a rich province and there is no reason in the world why they cannot respond positively to the lead that has been given by the Minister of State for Urban Affairs. We find that Saskatchewan has by and large been pretty responsive, but the policies of Saskatchewan and Manitoba have not been sufficiently far reaching so far as the Metis and the Indians are concerned. I think that with this policy we are entering a new era of responsiveness to the needs of the native people and I hope we can really do something with the new housing policy announced by the Minister of State for Urban Affairs.
I want to join a number of my colleagues who have spoken about the needs of Canadian cattlemen. I represent a constituency that has quite a large cattle population. I suppose the cattle population of British Columbia numbers up to half a million in peak periods. In my own riding it is perhaps up to 100,000. It is probably one of the constituencies with the highest cattle population in British Columbia.
That's lot of bull.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development
speechtext: I should say that a good bull sale is going on in Kamloops tonight. It is one of the best shows. Kamloops is the centre of the cattle industry in B.C. and we are proud of it. It means that $37 million to $40 million a year passes through the city of Kamloops from the cattle industry, which is pretty important. The cattlemen of Canada, and the cattlemen of B.C. in particular, have had a pretty tough time. I hope that the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Whelan), together with his colleague the Minister of Finance (Mr. Turner) who is here tonight-
He doesn't care.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development
speechtext:
-and the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce (Mr. Gillespie), have taken note of the real needs of cattlemen. Their needs are quite acute at this time, and I hope the government will see fit to impose a positive program of tariffs so that the situation of Canadian cattlemen will not be jeopardized any further. I know that the Minister of Agriculture has been responding in a positive way, since he became minister, to the needs of cattlemen and I believe that he will come through again.
I want to say a few words about the cattlemen in my own riding and cattlemen in British Columbia and expand upon why they have had such a difficult time. The winter of 1972 was a very difficult one. As a result, the hay crops were frozen out and a number of ranchers in the interior of B.C. had no hay last summer. Also, the dairy farmers found themselves short of hay because of the severe winter. The crops were frozen out and they did not have time to reseed. This was coupled with a very dry summer in the interior of B.C. The dairy farmers and ranchers in British Columbia were paying up to $110 a ton for hay this

winter. That has hit them very hard. I spoke to a number of the producers who were having to sell their herds. This is one of the worst things that they can do at a time of inflation; it means that in time the supply will not be there because many of the producers have sold their herds due to the severe shortage of hay.
In the few minutes that I have left I would like to touch upon another matter that has very much concerned the residents of Kamloops. A week or so ago CRTC, which is an independent commission, rendered a decision for the provision of cablevision to Kamloops. One might say that we should have been happy, but most of the people were not very happy with that decision. Many of them felt they were being treated as second-class citizens. The decision provided that the cablevision company could provide only one commercial non-Canadian channel. You can go up a little way to Merritt, 60 miles from Kamloops, and find that there they have access to all three commercial nonCanadian channels. If you go to Penticton, Kelowna, Cranbrook or Kimberley you will find that these places, all of which are not very far from Kamloops, have access to all the American networks. In Vancouver they have access to all the channels. But the CRTC in its wisdom decided that Kamloops could have only one commercial American channel. The people of Kamloops feel very strongly about this decision. They feel it is the wrong policy and the wrong decision.
Hear, hear!

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development
speechtext: Why should they be treated any differently from the people who are in Kelowna, Penticton, Merritt and Vancouver? If big, bad American television is not good for us, then it should not be any good for the people on the coast either.

Mr. Speaker, I will commence by extending the traditional compliment to the mover and the seconder of the address in reply to Speech from the Throne, the hon. member for Spadina (Mr. Stol-lery) and the hon. member for Sherbrooke (Mr. Pelletier). However, I will not follow the usual tradition of speaking this evening about matters affecting particular concerns in my constituency, although I have good cause for doing so particularly since in this session we have embarked upon a study of legislation affecting our two northern ridings, Yukon and the Northwest Territories, which is rather important to the people of those territories. I could speak about the bill introduced by the Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development (Mr. Chretien) today which will bring about what he is going to characterize as certain large steps forward, but there will be an opportunity to debate these matters later.
I was somewhat surprised today at the reluctance of the President of the Privy Council (Mr. MacEachen) to go ahead with the introduction of the bill to amend the British North America Act 1867-1965 in order to provide two more seats in the other place which undoubtedly are to be occupied by one appointee from the Yukon and one from the Northwest Territories. This would be in keeping with the recommendation of the joint committee of the House and the other place on the constitution which held
The Address-Mr. Nielsen
hearings all over the country a few years ago. I am glad to see that legislation coming forward. I think members will find it to be almost verbatim with a bill that has been standing on the order paper in my name for a good many years.
Rather than deal with those matters concerning the ridings of Yukon and the Northwest Territories, as opportunities will be provided in the future to speak about them, I want to speak about something that is nearer to the hearts of all Canadians. That is inflation, taxes and the ever increasing cost of living in the country and the part the government is playing in contributing to the absolutely uncontrollable situation that confronts us today.
It is a fact that in the years 1968-69 to 1974-75 the percentage increase in the main estimates is 103.5 per cent. They went from $7,170.3 million in 1964-65 to $22,022.9 million in 1974-75. I am happy to see the President of the Treasury Board (Mr. Drury) and the Minister of Finance (Mr. Turner) in their places tonight because some of these figures perhaps have not been presented to them before in this fashion. One might call them Peter and Paul. The lid is off; the Minister of Finance obviously cannot control the spending of his colleagues, and the President of the Treasury Board is obviously unable to bring his influence to bear.
In the last year, 1973-74 to 1974-75, the increase in the main estimates was 9.7 per cent. One of the greatest areas of wasteful government spending is in departmental information services. We all recall that when Information Canada was set up it was supposed to do away with the information services hitherto provided in each of the departments. It was supposed to be a central place where information would be available to all Canadians. Now we see that the public relations offices in the departments have not been diminished at all but have been increasing. Even after the advent of Information Canada in 1970 there has been a multiplication of costs rather than a reduction.
The latest statistics of February, 1974, reveal that there were 747 publicists on the federal government payroll, with 378 openings, for a total staff of 1,125. The number of government-owned buildings in the national capital region alone is over 600, and buildings leased by the government either in whole or in part stand at over 150. The value of the annual leases has jumped 50 per cent to $29 million in the last five years.
A return which was tabled to a written question revealed that in the fiscal year 1970-71, the total-and here are some statistics: I saw the Minister of Finance smiling a moment ago but perhaps these might be drawn to the attention of his colleagues because they are rather embarrassing-entertainment bill for the year 1970-71 for government departments and agencies, including the Prime Minister's office, amounted to $1,892,194.
The breakdown for travelling expenses in the same year was very interesting. In 1970-71, travelling expenses for all departments, including the Prime Minister's office but excluding the agencies of the Crown, which are plethoric-to hit a few of the highlights-were, Department of the Environment, $7,201,886.15. One might ask where they went. The Department of National Health and Welfare, just for travelling, spent $3,987,377. That department is very active in the entertainment field and spent $49,050.

March 11, 1974
The Address-Mr. Nielsen
The Department of Transport, which one would think could get around less expensively, spent $6,970,189; and the Postmaster General, whose department has one of the greatest deficits in government, spent $3,004,970.23. In entertainment, the Department of the Environment spent $55,716.83. Sir, spending in this government is entirely out of control.
How about that $20 billion farce-the budget?

Yes, and one might ask about the $8,000 cabinet meeting held last year. Rather than choosing one of two more than adequate cabinet rooms on parliament hill or one of the Prime Minister's establishments, the Prime Minister decided to hold a one-day cabinet meeting at the O'Brien estate, an NCC property. It took the NCC two weeks and between $6,000 and $8,000 to put the house in shape. These expenses did not include the cost of trucking furniture from the Conference Centre, security men, the luncheon caterer, cars to transport the ministers to and from the meeting, or the time of the Privy Council staff dispatched to provide wood for the three fireplaces.
I should like to go into another area of uncontrollable inflation, Mr. Speaker, namely, government growth. In 1969, when the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) pledged to freeze expansion of government personnel, the size of the public service was 230,000 excluding commissions, corporations, the armed forces and contract employees. Since then the public service has increased by over 57,000. In the Toronto area alone the increase was from 18,450 in 1971 to over 20,000 in 1972; in the Ottawa-Hull area from 66,000 in 1971 to 75,000 in 1974, and in the Montreal area from 23,400 in 1971 to 25,400 in 1972.
There was a constant barrage of criticism of the government for these uncontrollable increases. If put in terms of a monthly increase, it becomes more staggering. Who in his right mind would say that it is reasonable to expect growth in the civil service of this country of some 1,300 per month?
Drury.
I suppose the President of the Treasury Board and the Minister of Finance think that is a normal growth rate.
It is research staff for the Tories.

Let me speak now about ministerial absences. We are faced with the highest inflation rate, the highest tax rate and the highest cost of living in the history of the country. The government called for an extended Christmas recess, ostensibly for the purpose of working out a legislative program which would meet these crucial problems. Then we found in the last week of February that the only minister of the Crown in Ottawa to be dignified with the rank of acting prime minister was the nineteenth ranking member of the cabinet, the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs (Mr. Gray). He was the only one who could be found. What a way to guide a country!

This happened when most of his colleagues were enjoying the sun in southern retreats and the Prime Minister was skiing in St. Moritz. I do not suggest that ministers should be begrudged holidays, not at all; but it is a bit much, when both unemployment and inflation are on the rise, that the only minister who can be found at his desk in Ottawa is the nineteenth ranking member of the cabinet, the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs.
Where were you?
I was working in the Yukon, not sunning myself and getting lovely and brown as the Minister of Finance did.
You have to pick up your mail sometimes, Erik.

As Mr. W. A. Wilson said in the Montreal Star, referring to the energy conference of last January 22 and 23:
Conferences that fail, broadcast the lack of preparation that went into them. The rush from the failed conference to the ski slopes and the beaches suggests strange orders of priorities.
There we see one reason for the uncontrollable situation which we face. Government members are simply not doing their jobs. Would not the cabinet have been better advised spending their recess in preparing legislation to get at the roots of the major problem facing Canada today, unemployment and inflation, rather than vacationing or spending their time attending foreign conferences which should be given a much lower priority?
Sir, I do not have time to put the rest of these disgusting statistics on record. All I can say is that the sooner the government leaves the treasury benches opposite, the sooner there will be some sanity in this country.
